The Homeric question is a scholarly debate that revolves around the identity of the poet or poets behind the Homeric epics, namely the "Iliad" and the "Odyssey." It also delves into the relationship between the figure known as "Homer" and these epic works. This discussion became prominent in the 19th century, acting as a key divergence between two contrasting schools of thought: the Analysts and the Unitarians. The origins of the Homeric question can be traced back to the 18th century, a period marked by a burgeoning interest in popular ballads and folktales. During this time, scholars began to recognize that the Homeric epics were likely transmitted orally before they were eventually written down. This realization suggested that the texts may have been compiled much later than the traditional dating of "Homer" himself. One prominent participant in this discussion was the Italian philosopher Giambattista Vico, who claimed that the epics were not the work of a single gifted poet but instead represented the cultural output of an entire community. In his 1769 "Essay on the Original Genius and Writings of Homer," Robert Wood contended that Homer was uneducated and that the epics had been passed down through oral tradition. However, Wood's comparison of Homer to the supposed Scottish oral poet Ossian, whose works were published by James Macpherson in 1765, has since been discredited, as Ossian was later revealed to be a fabrication by Macpherson. The German scholar Friedrich August Wolf was instrumental in progressing the Homeric question. In his critique of Emmanuel-Pierre-Louis de Villoison's 1788 edition of the A and B scholia on the "Iliad," Wolf recognized that the scholia offered definitive proof of the oral transmission of the poems. Building on this, Wolf published his "Prolegomena ad Homerum" in 1795, in which he proposed that the Homeric poems were composed in the mid-10th century BCE and transmitted orally before being written down. This work played a major role in shaping the later discussion regarding the Homeric question.

"A Dirge" by James Russell Lowell is a poignant reflection on the life and death of a poet, whose heart has found eternal peace beneath the cold earth. The poet is laid to rest beneath the rustling green trees, the warm hum of bees, and the drowsy clover. A smooth gurgle of a blue stream murmurs over his grave, as the sun shines down from the blue sky above. Three paces from the silver strand, the poet is gently laid in the fine, white sand, clutching a lily in his hand. His body is not confined by the coarse earth or the gloomy coffin-lid. Instead, sweet birds sing at his sunny burial, and meek forget-me-nots grow where his large, blue eyes once lay hidden beneath the turf. The poet's spirit is free, his heart full of love, truth, forgiveness, and compassion. He dwells in mysteries, with shadows of serener skies lingering in his eyes. His great heart is filled with hope and youth, tiding over the waves of want, woe, and wrong. He strives to win the world with his angelic song, despite the challenges he faces. The poet's sin is to see and hear beyond today's dim hemisphere, into a life more true and clear. He longs for the light of the new world, yet he is left heartbroken. His brethren stand in fear, unable to hear the sounds of the land that the poet's quick ear caught long ago. The poet does not seek the poet's wreath, yet he wins it too soon. Beneath it lies scorn, loneliness, and death, gnawing at his brain with burning teeth. He is full of nobleness, whose life-blood is to bless, yet he must bandy words with wickedness and haggle with hunger and distress. The poet's spirit soars high above the spheres, seeking its starry peers. It comes not back to face the jeers of brothers who denied it. Star-crowned, the poet possesses the deeps of God, and his white body sleeps where the lone pine forever keeps patient watch beside it. In "Sonnet to My Mother" by T. Holley Chivers, the poet expresses his deep love and gratitude for his mother's unwavering love and care from the moment he was born. His mother's soul dwells in his heart, nurturing him and shaping him into a semblance of herself. The poet acknowledges his mother as his first and last friend, lost in her love. "Boston Ramblings" by Miss Leslie explores the city's strong attachment to its history and traditions. Bostonians have long cherished the relics and memories of their early settlers and the revolution. However, modern improvements and the pursuit of financial gain are gradually replacing the veneration for the places and things connected with their history. The author notes the disappearance of many antiquated and perhaps unsightly structures that once held a sense of poetry, romance, and quaintness. New and more profitable buildings have taken their place, leaving only a few vestiges of the past. The author laments the loss of the "old familiar faces" of these time-honored habitations. Fortunately, Faneuil Hall remains protected by the city's charter, ensuring that it will never be sold or its ground appropriated for any other purpose. The edifice still stands nearly as it was when the walls of its chief apartment echoed with the acclamations of the people discussing the principles that led to their self-emancipation from the sway of oppression.

The figure within the painting is immense, her flowing gown highlighting her imposing stature. She simpers in profile, her elongated chin contrasting with her precariously slanted posture. The lamplight, emanating from below as if she stands on a grand platform, casts peculiar shadows across her expansive face. In the background, the outline of musicians, dressed in black with white shirts, appears against the wall, their shadows blending with posters, guitars, and stained fingerprints. This artwork captures a vivid sense of reality with remarkable breadth and boldness. However, its flaw lies in its unsettling effect on the viewer, which is unfortunate given that the sight of a graceful, passionate dancer is not inherently displeasing. "El Jaleo" leans toward unattractiveness, and aside from the dancer's bulky skirts, it fails to convey a feeling of calm. This is sharply contrasting with the appealing, dark-hued figure in the Tangerine-themed painting shown at the 1880 Salon. This piece, born from the artist's visit to the African coast during his time in Spain, depicts a woman standing on a rug beneath a grand white Moorish arch. Her hands raise her voluminous drapery, casting her head in shadow, with only her painted eyes and brows visible above her bandaged mouth. She looks down at the fumes from a lovely censer or chafing-dish on the floor, her silent reflection and pearl-hued garments beneath the shining plastered arcade both enchanting and distressing the observer. The painting is exquisite, a radiant interplay of whites, a testament to the artist's skill in differentiating similar yet distinct tones. When dividing the accolades Mr. Sargent has garnered for his finest works, it is crucial to recognize the merit of his 1882 painting of four little girls, which was exhibited the following year to much acclaim. The artist has created a vivid, subdued French interior, offering a complete portrayal of a family's playful environment, employing an unusual approach that avoids the conventional symmetric placement of figures. The scene is viewed as a whole, yet the children in their white pinafores (painted with such power and poetry) stand out with a personal life. Two sisters stand hand in hand at the back, accompanied by a pair of towering, ornate jars that seem to share in the life of the painting. The porcelain and the children's aprons gleam together, while a mirror in the background catches the light. Another girl, with abundant hair and slim legs, stands to the left, and the youngest sits on the floor, playing with her doll. The naturalness of the composition, the loveliness of the complete effect, the light, free execution, and the sense of assimilated secrets and instinct and knowledge at play make this painting an astonishing achievement for a young artist of twenty-six. Mr. Sargent is occasionally faulted for lacking "finish," yet if "finish" denotes the highest expression of touch, "The Hall with the Four Children" may function as a lasting example. If the portrait of the Spanish dancer demonstrates the limitations of Impressionist technique, this painting exemplifies the successes it can attain. Like the young lady holding a flower, this piece encourages the viewer to reflect on what still awaits the artist. It raises the question of whether it is advantageous for an artist to master their craft so early in life, potentially leading to a sense of irresponsibility or a lack of reverence. Such reflections belong to those who remain critical even in their most sincere appreciations, doubting that it might be preferable for an artist to struggle with unresolved challenges. When this is not the case, the question of the artist's future becomes more focused. "What will he do with it?" we inquire, alluding to the artist's refined abilities. It becomes a question of accountability, and we expect the artist to meet a greater standard. This applies to Mr. Sargent; his broad understanding of painting might lead him to manipulate it or perhaps misuse it. Though he has painted few subjects other than portraits, his experimentation and risk-taking set him apart from those who adhere strictly to the literal. Mr. Sargent's work has been predominantly represented by portraits, but there are a few subject-pictures that stand out. A small painting exhibited at the Grosvenor Gallery, for instance, depicts a group of Venetian girls engaged in humble household tasks in the dim hall of an old palazzo. The light filtering through the shutters illuminates the scagliola pavement, and the vegetables they work with are painted with such enchanting detail that they appear as valuable as magnified pearls. The figures are remarkably natural and vivid, and the painter's touch is light and fine, evoking the small, familiar Venetian realities without succumbing to the clichés that often plague depictions of Italy. The National Register of Historic Places is a list that recognizes historic districts, sites, buildings, and properties in the United States. It relies on the standards of National Historic Landmarks, which also outline exclusions and exceptions to those exclusions. The register serves as a form of governmental acknowledgment, but it is primarily an honorary status with some federal financial incentives. Inclusion in the National Register automatically encompasses all National Historic Landmarks, as well as historic areas managed by the National Park Service. This comprises National Historic Sites (NHS), National Historical Parks, National Military Parks/Battlefields, National Memorials, and specific National Monuments. In some instances, historic sites outside the United States that have a connection to the country, such as the American Legation in Tangier, Morocco, are also listed. Listing in the National Register does not impose any restrictions on private property owners concerning the use of their property. However, some states and municipalities may have laws that come into effect when a property is listed in the register. When federal funds or a federal permit process is involved, Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966 comes into effect. This section requires the involved federal agency to evaluate the effects of its activities on historic resources. The National Register of Historic Places and the associated criteria aim to preserve and protect the country's rich historical heritage, ensuring that these significant sites are recognized and maintained for future generations.

The idea of "creaturely freedom" as it relates to libertarianism is a subject of discussion in both philosophy and theology. Molinists, who advocate for the compatibility of divine omniscience and human free will, accept that creatures are free in the libertarian sense. However, they argue against the notion that counterfactuals of creaturely freedom lack truth values, as some critics suggest. Some philosophers and theologians who raise the grounding objection suggest that instead of counterfactuals of freedom being definitively true, it is the probable counterfactuals that are actually true. This means that rather than stating, "God knows that in circumstance C, creature X will freely do A," it would be more accurate to say, "God knows that in circumstances C, creature X would probably do A." However, Edward Wierenga has pointed out that probable counterfactuals are also contingent truths and thus face the same grounding objection. Molinists have offered two main responses to this argument. First, William Lane Craig argues that for a counterfactual of freedom to be true, it is not necessary for the events they refer to actually exist. Instead, it is sufficient that they would exist under the specified conditions. This perspective suggests that if God were to create multiple universes in various dimensions, granting libertarian free will to individuals in these universes, counterfactuals of freedom could be grounded based on the events occurring in these different universes. The second response to the grounding objection involves questioning why God would need to create such universes to know how events would unfold. Critics argue that the very nature of how events would turn out could serve as the grounding for statements about how they would turn out. This approach invites additional debates and challenges in the philosophical and theological conversations regarding divine foreknowledge and human freedom.

Petrofiction, also known as oil fiction, is a literary genre that centers on the significance of petroleum in society and its influence on the human experience. The term was initially coined by Amitav Ghosh in 1992 during his review of Abdul Rahman Munif's novel "Cities of Salt." Ghosh sought to categorize literature focusing on the petroleum industry and its societal effects, especially emphasizing the scarcity of works addressing the "oil encounters" between oil-producing and oil-consuming countries. In 2012, Imre Szeman expanded the definition of petrofiction in an editorial for a special edition of the American Book Review. Szeman proposed that the genre encompasses all works that examine "the important role played by oil in contemporary society." This broader scope allows for a more comprehensive understanding of how oil shapes various aspects of modern life. The 2000s and 2010s saw a surge in petrofiction works, driven by growing concerns about climate change and the concept of peak oil. Consequently, the term has come to be extensively used in literary criticism for examining fiction that challenges society's dependence on a petroleum-based economy and the culture it generates. While critics originally aimed to find works centered on the oil industry before "Cities of Salt," petrofiction has become more prominent in non-Western literature. This genre provides a distinctive viewpoint on the ways in which engagement with oil relates to other significant matters in the Global South. Some scholars have drawn connections between petrofiction and the emergence of climate fiction, as both genres address the challenges and concerns arising from the Anthropocene era. By exploring the consequences of human activities on the environment, these literary works encourage readers to reflect on the need for sustainable development and environmental stewardship. Notable examples of petrofiction include Abdul Rahman Munif's "Cities of Salt" series, which examines the experiences of individuals impacted by the oil industry within a fictionalized Arabian Peninsula context. Other works in this genre continue to shed light on the complex relationship between society, petroleum, and the environment, fostering a deeper understanding of our world's dependence on oil and its implications for the future.

As the travelers descended from their vantage point, the view of Mary's River came into sight. With only two miles left of their journey, the Captain began to sing an old song of their time, his voice as robust as that of a professional singer: "The moon, the moon, the jolly moon, And a jolly old queen she is! She has wandered o' nights for a thousand years, With the finest company. Sing, Hic and hoc sumus nocturno, Hurrah for the jolly old moon!" "Why, Garret, vintner, are you asleep, man?" the Captain inquired. "Why don't you join in the chorus?" "To your hand, Captain," Weasel exclaimed, shaking off his drowsiness and singing out the refrain— "Hic and hoc sumus nocturno, Hurrah for the jolly old moon!" which he repeated with enthusiasm at each repetition. Dauntrees continued: "She trails a royal following, And keeps a merry mad court, With her chirping boys that walk in the shade, And wake when the bailiff's asleep. Sing, Hic and hoc sumus nocturno, Hurrah for the jolly old moon! "Master Owl is her chancellor, And the bat is his servant; They tell no tales of what they see, But wink when we turn up the can. Sing, Hic and hoc sumus nocturno, Hurrah for the jolly old moon! "Her chorister is Goodman Frog, With a glow-worm for his torch; And all who would make court to her, Must, in truth, be ready to drink. Sing, Hic and hoc sumus nocturno, Hurrah for the jolly old moon!" The song had barely ended—extended by several noisy repetitions of the chorus—when the group arrived at the Fort's gate. The sleepy sentinel opened the door at the Captain's call, and soon, the weary adventurers were enjoying the deep sleep of the truly tired. CHAPTER XII. There remains a rugged trunk, dismembered and unsightly, Waiting for the final bolt to burst And shatter it into splinters. THE DOOM OF DEVORGOIL. The shore of the Chesapeake between Cape St. Michael—known by early settlers as the northern headland at the mouth of the Potomac—and the Patuxent, is typically flat, marked by a clear, pebbly beach. This shoreline, spanning about twenty miles, is intersected by a single creek, that of St. Jerome, which flows into the bay some five or six miles north of the Potomac. The beach, occasionally interrupted by small elevations that would not be considered hills elsewhere but are notable in this area, rises just enough to offer a clear view over the expansive waters and to distinguish the inland landscape for mariners navigating up the bay. At certain points, these gentle hills end abruptly at the tide in the form of a cliff, while at others, they form a knoll that slopes down to the beach, covered in grass. This feature can be seen near St. Jerome's, where the slope descends steeply to the tide level, leaving a strip of low ground about fifty paces wide between its base and the ordinary waterline. It was on this flat area that, in ancient times, stood the dwelling of Paul Kelpy the fisherman—a long, low building made of deal boards, constructed in the shape of a warehouse or magazine. A quarter of a mile along the beach, hidden under the brow of the slope and nearly obscured by the natural shrubbery, stood a humble cottage. Its low height allowed a man of average stature to touch the roof eaves while standing at the door. The cottage was small, with only two rooms, the largest of which was no more than ten feet square. It was constructed from hewn logs, and its door, strengthened by thick nails and a sturdy padlock, offered protection against all but the most persistent intruders. A small enclosure surrounded the cottage, providing space for a few common garden plants that were well-tended. A few acres on the higher plain above the bank showed signs of cultivation, and fishing equipment scattered around, along with a skiff on the sand, indicated the livelihood of the cottage's occupant. The day prior to the events of our story, roughly an hour before sunset, a gentle drizzle accompanied by a consistent wind from the northeast created a cool, somber atmosphere over the scene, amplifying the feeling of isolation. A slender column of smoke ascending from the cottage's chimney indicated that someone was living there, as evidenced by the large, cross-facened mastiff-bitch peeking out from beneath the roof, serving as a gloomy protector of this lonely location. The waves, driven by the flood tide, crashed almost at the cottage's door with a ceaseless, harsh roar.

Relativism, a philosophical concept that suggests varying perspectives may be equally valid, has been criticized by notable philosophers such as Hilary Putnam and Susan Haack, who consider it to be misguided. John Dewey, in his work "The Quest for Certainty," criticized what he termed "the philosophical fallacy." He argued that philosophers often take certain categories, such as the mental and the physical, for granted without recognizing that these are nominal concepts created to address specific issues. This oversight can lead to metaphysical and conceptual confusion. Examples of this fallacy include the "ultimate Being" in Hegelian philosophy, the belief in a "realm of value," and the notion that logic, as an abstraction from concrete thought, is disconnected from the action of concrete thinking. David L. Hildebrand captured the problem, noting that neglecting the particular roles of inquiry has caused both realists and idealists to impose the outcomes of thorough abstraction upon experience. Pragmatists, from the beginning, aimed to reform philosophy and align it more closely with the scientific method. They argued that idealist and realist philosophies often portrayed human knowledge as lying outside the reach of scientific inquiry. According to pragmatists, these philosophies frequently depended on either a Kantian phenomenology or theories of knowledge and truth based on correspondence. Pragmatists criticized the former for its a priorism and the latter for its reliance on the concept of correspondence.

The concept of "human wisdom" has been a subject of debate and contemplation throughout history. In 1920, historian J. B. Bury posited that the ultimate goal of human development for many is a society where all inhabitants enjoy a perfectly happy existence. However, he also acknowledged that it is impossible to prove whether humanity's unknown destination is indeed desirable. The idea of progress, Bury argued, is akin to concepts like Providence or personal immortality—it can be seen as either true or false, and its validity cannot be definitively proven or disproven. Belief in progress, therefore, is ultimately a matter of faith. In the 1980s, postmodernist thought began to challenge the grand claims made by modernizers. This movement cast doubt on the concept of social advancement, examining the deeds and ideals of radical modernizers such as Joseph Stalin and Mao Zedong, who are typically regarded as authoritarian leaders with an inaccurate perception of progress. Postmodernists argue that the 19th and 20th-century notions of progress, both within capitalism and Marxism, are flawed. They believe that these ideologies place too much emphasis on technological advancements and material wealth, neglecting the importance of inner happiness and mental peace. According to postmodernist thought, the concepts of dystopia and utopia are essentially the same, representing overarching grand narratives with unattainable conclusions. In summary, the idea of progress has been a topic of ongoing discussion and debate. While some view it as a necessary and desirable aspect of human development, others question its validity and implications. The postmodernist viewpoint provides a critical analysis of conventional ideas about progress, advocating for a reassessment of what genuinely represents societal development.

The narrative surrounding Daniel Home and his supposed supernatural abilities has been a subject of intrigue and skepticism for many years. It is said that Home possessed an extraordinary power that allowed him to transfer this energy to others, a claim that has been met with both fascination and disbelief. However, a more practical viewpoint proposes that the occurrences linked to Home can be accounted for by more ordinary explanations. Take, for instance, the incident involving a live coal. While some might contend that Home's capacity to manage a burning coal without harm demonstrates his superhuman abilities, a more reasonable explanation can be found in the characteristics of the coal itself. It is not uncommon for certain parts of a coal to be less active, or "dead," allowing for safe handling. Furthermore, the description of Mr. Hall's white hair appearing "silvery" against the coal suggests that the coal was not glowing, indicating that it was likely not as hot as one might assume. The involvement of Sir William Crookes, a renowned scientist, adds a layer of credibility to these events. However, it is important to remember that even the most learned individuals can be deceived. Crookes' account of witnessing Home placing his hands in the fire lacks the precision and detail one would expect from a scientific observer. His description of Home handling a "bright red" coal is also questionable, as it does not account for the possibility that the coal may not have been uniformly hot. The narrative then shifts to the subject of musical phenomena, with Home once again at the center of the discussion. His alleged ability to induce spirits to play an accordion while he held it is a fascinating claim, but one that is easily explained through sleight of hand and deception. The circumstances in which these performances occurred—typically in low light and from behind a curtain—offer considerable chances for deception. The use of a cage to contain the accordion during a séance led by Sir W. Crookes presents a more challenging scenario. However, the absence of any witness to the keys moving during the performance raises questions about the authenticity of the event. The possibility of a hidden musical box or the use of hooks and loops to manipulate the accordion cannot be discounted. The account of Mrs. Annie Eva Fay, another medium who asserted she communicated with spirits via music, additionally demonstrates the possibility of deceit in such presentations. Her séances, which involved her sitting in a circle with a bell and a guitar, were designed to create the illusion of supernatural activity. The incorporation of darkness along with her husband, "Colonel" Fay, within the circle implies that the pair could have been collaborating to produce the semblance of ghostly musicians. The discovery that Mrs. Fay's performances might be recreated using straightforward techniques, including tape manipulation and concealed items, raises questions about the validity of her assertions. The fact that she offered to reveal her secrets for a fee further undermines her credibility. In conclusion, while the stories of Daniel Home and other mediums may be captivating, it is essential to approach these accounts with a critical eye. The use of deception, sleight of hand, and the manipulation of the senses are common tools employed by those seeking to create the illusion of supernatural phenomena. As with any historical account, it is crucial to consider the context, the motivations of the individuals involved, and the possibility of alternative explanations before accepting these tales as evidence of the paranormal.

As the solemn silence was broken by the declaration "Condemned to death," a collective murmur of compassion rippled through the crowd. This was followed by a hushed silence as the rest of the document was read out. Another murmur arose upon hearing the sentences: Maroncelli to hard imprisonment for twenty years, and Pellico for fifteen. The Captain signaled for us to descend, and we cast one last glance around before returning to the court-yard. We ascended the grand staircase and were led back to the room from which we had been taken. The manacles were removed, and we were soon escorted back to San Michele. CHAPTER LIV The prisoners who had been sentenced before us had already departed for Lubiana and Spielberg, accompanied by a police commissary. He was now expected to return and guide us to our destination. However, a month passed before he arrived. To distract myself, I spent my time conversing and listening to others, including Maroncelli, who read me some of his literary works, and I reciprocated by sharing my own. One evening, I read my play "Ester d’Engaddi" from the window to Canova, Rezia, and Armari, and the following night, "Iginia d’Asti." However, at night, I became restless and miserable, struggling to sleep. I was both eager and apprehensive to learn how my family had received the news of my misfortune. Eventually, I received a letter from my father, which revealed that my last letter to him had not been sent as I had requested from the Inquisitor. This caused me great distress, as my father had been under the impression that I would be released, only to read the dreadful sentence in the Milan Gazette. I could not express the contempt and anger I felt upon learning that my letter had been withheld, and I deeply empathized with the suffering of my family. Although I now believe there was no malice in this delay, I still view it as a cruel act, an eager, infernal desire to cause my loved ones immense pain. I was further enraged to learn that my companions were planning to celebrate Easter week before their departure. As for me, I could not fathom the idea of forgiveness, and the thought of participating in such a celebration seemed impossible. CHAPTER LV Finally, the German commissioner arrived and informed us that we would be departing within two days. He also provided some reassuring information: after returning from Spielberg, he had met with the Emperor in Vienna, who told him that our punishment would not extend for twenty-four hours, but only twelve. This was meant to signify that the pain would be divided, or half the punishment remitted. Although this information was not officially communicated to us, there was no reason to doubt the commissioner's words, especially since he was open about it and it was known to the entire commission. However, I could not find solace in this news. To me, seven and a half years in chains and solitude seemed no different from fifteen; I believed it would be impossible to survive such a long period. My health had deteriorated, with severe chest pains and a persistent cough, leading me to fear that my lungs were affected. I ate little and struggled to digest what I consumed. Our departure occurred on the night of the 25th of March. We were allowed to bid farewell to our friend, Cesare Armari. A sbirro chained us in a transverse manner, linking the right hand to the left foot, making escape impossible. We boarded a gondola, with the guards rowing us towards Fusina. Upon arrival, we found two boats prepared for us. Rezia and Canova were placed in one, while Maroncelli and I were in the other. The commissary accompanied two of the prisoners, and an under-commissary accompanied the others. Six or seven armed police guards completed our convoy, some in the boats and others in the Vetturino's box. Being forced to leave one's country due to misfortune is always painful, but to be torn away in chains, exiled to a harsh climate, and confined to solitary dungeons for days, hours, and years, is a fate so terrible that words cannot convey its full horror. Before we crossed the Alps, I realized how much my country meant to me. The sympathy we received from people of all ranks was an irresistible appeal to my affection and gratitude. In every city, village, and even the humblest of dwellings, news of our conviction had spread, and we were anticipated. In various locations, the commissioners and guards struggled to disperse the crowds that had gathered around us. It was remarkable to witness the benevolent and humane feelings expressed on our behalf. In Udine, we experienced a touching incident. Upon arriving at the inn, the commissary ordered the courtyard door to be closed to keep the people at bay.

Eschenbach's "Parzival," the Ethiopian national epic "Kebra Nagast," the tales of Prester John, and the imagery of Chartres Cathedral are some of the historical and mythological sources examined in the book. The author, Graham Hancock, posits that the Knights Templar sought the lost Ark of the Covenant and other relics at the Temple Mount in Jerusalem during the 12th century. It is suggested that an Ethiopian king in exile, possibly Lalibela, made contact with the Knights Templar while residing in Jerusalem during that time. This hypothesis is supported by the architectural legacy of Lalibela, particularly the Church of Saint George, which is intriguing in the context of Gothic architecture's development. The Ethiopian Church, concerned about the potential loss of the Ark to the Knights Templar, allegedly dispatched emissaries to Pope Clement V in 1306. The book argues that the Catholic Church's apprehension regarding the Knights Templar gaining the Ark's power was a contributing factor in Pope Clement V's decision to initiate the prosecution and arrest of the Knights Templar in 1307. The book achieved commercial success but was met with unfavorable reviews from critics. Jonathan Kirsch from the Los Angeles Times referred to it as a mix of travel writing, genuine adventure, and a mystery thriller, yet mainly labeled it as amateurish scholarship paired with a creative storyline, similar to sharing ghost tales by a campfire. Desmond Ryan of the Philadelphia Inquirer humorously questioned the extent of the author's speculation.

Noir fiction, a genre characterized by its dark, moody atmosphere and morally complex characters, has a rich history that spans several decades and continents. Pioneered by American authors such as Elliott Chaze, Charles Williams, Gil Brewer, Harry Whittington, Peter Rabe, and Lionel White, alongside David Goodis and Jim Thompson, this literary movement has evolved and expanded over time. In the 1980s, Black Lizard, an American publisher, played a significant role in reviving interest in noir fiction by re-releasing many classic works. Today, Akashic Books continues to celebrate the genre with a diverse collection of noir short-story anthologies. The noir genre has also found a strong foothold in Europe, with notable authors such as Jean-Claude Izzo and Massimo Carlotto contributing to its growth. According to Italian publisher Sandro Ferri, "Mediterranean noir" stands out for its exploration of the dual nature of Mediterranean life. These novels often depict Mediterranean cities as places that have been marred by crime, yet still possess a captivating charm. The genre is marked by a sense of duality, juxtaposing the Mediterranean lifestyle's emphasis on fine wine, food, friendship, and conviviality with the harsh realities of violence, corruption, greed, and power abuses. Among contemporary authors who write in both the hardboiled and noir styles, James Ellroy is particularly prominent. He characterizes noir as "the most scrutinized branch of the hard-boiled school of fiction," and emphasizes its attraction through the "thrill of moral surrender and the surrender to sensuality." Ellroy also recognizes the societal relevance of noir, pointing out its focus on major topics like race, class, gender, and systemic concerns. Noir fiction maintains its lasting appeal due to its capacity to explore the intricacies of human nature and society, providing readers with an engaging and intellectually stimulating encounter.

Horace Townsend, known affectionately as "H. T.," emerged from a perilous ordeal with a renewed vigor, his cheeks flushed with warmth and his body imbued with a newfound strength. He stood, barefoot and clad only in his shirt-sleeves, his hair plastered to his head and his clothes clinging to him, an unassuming figure yet one that would inspire any artist's admiration—a man who had just braved a great danger out of selfless benevolence. Margaret Hayley, noting his tall and upright stance, perceived not the faintest suggestion of anything lacking in romance. Perhaps to her eyes, his dusky complexion seemed to radiate a kind of sacred light, a beacon for her admiration, a stark contrast to the feelings she had recently been obliged to express. It was only such a profound estimation that could explain her subsequent actions, which, for a woman of her considerable pride, led to a terrible internal conflict that made any calamity that might have occurred in the waters of the Pool seem like a mercy in comparison. Halstead Rowan, assured by his admiration for his new friend's conduct and not eager to express it hastily, had performed what his wounded hand permitted—jumping across the stream to recover the discarded shoes and coat from the rock where they rested. While the rest of the group, with the exception of the distraught Mrs. Brooks Cunninghame, who was still tending to her barely revived son, gathered around the new hero to offer their thanks and congratulations, it was Margaret Hayley who took his hand. Ignoring the disapproving scowl of Captain Hector Coles, she said, "I do not know, sir, by what name to thank you—" "I believe I am right in calling you Miss Hayley," he replied, his voice still somewhat weak and tremulous. "My name is Horace Townsend, and I am a lawyer from Cincinnati." Thus, the mystery of the initials was solved, and we can now refer to him by his full name, as those who had noticed the initials but not taken the trouble to learn his full name from the arrival book at the office had done. "I was only half intentionally the cause of your dangerous situation, Mr. Townsend," Margaret continued, "and yet I cannot regret the liberty I took, for it may have saved a life that would have been lost, and allowed me to witness an act of selfless generosity that I will never forget, nor fail to honor for as long as I live." "You do me too much honor," he responded, his voice now a bit steadier. "I have done nothing more than expose my weakness. There was no danger to me in the water, as I am a capable swimmer and should be able to dive well. However, I must have stayed under too long, for I could not find the child immediately, and the cold water undoubtedly affected me after getting warm from climbing over the logs. That is all, and I truly hope we can all forget this unpleasant incident, as I certainly will once I have found some dry clothes." He spoke pleasantly, yet without the carefree cheerfulness that characterized his rival of the day—the hero of the bear-stakes. As he finished speaking, he bowed and turned away, suggesting that the conversation had reached its conclusion. Margaret Hayley also moved away and rejoined her escort. Halstead Rowan approached with the coat and shoes, and as he placed them on the rock at Townsend's feet, he grasped his hand with his unwounded one, conveying a deep sense of respect and admiration. "I am nowhere!" he exclaimed. "I challenged you over that log, but you have gone where I would not like to follow, and done it for a noble cause, while mine was merely a prank. And by the way—" They were now a little apart from the others, and Rowan spoke in a low voice, "do you know where your head lay when you came to?" "Hush! For heaven's sake, hush!" Townsend responded urgently, his expression prompting Rowan to immediately cease the conversation. The company soon began to ascend the steps, carrying the revived boy and accompanying his mother. Townsend managed to put on the discarded shoes over his wet stockings, donned his coat, and joined the rear-guard with minimal assistance. Despite the discomfort of his continued dampness, he was undoubtedly consoled by the thought that he had survived a plunge into the Pool where few men had ventured and emerged alive, and perhaps even more so by other, more complex reflections. An hour later, the entire group had returned to the Profile House, where Horace Townsend, now known by his full name, enjoyed a dry change of clothes, a slight headache, and a nap that left him refreshed as if he had bathed in the Pool for health reasons.

"Extending MARC for Subject Access," edited by Toni Petersen and Pat Molholt, is a publication by G.K. Hall that delves into the use of MARC (Machine-Readable Cataloging) for subject access in libraries. The book includes several papers on visual resources, such as "Access to Diverse Collections in University Settings: the Berkeley Dilemma" by Howard Besser and Maryly Snow, and "Visual Depictions and the Use of MARC: A View from the Trenches of Slide Librarianship" by Maryly Snow, both published in 1990. In 1991, Tim Berners-Lee began working on a hypertext graphical-user-interface (GUI) and coined the term "World Wide Web" for his program. That same year, "Facilities Standards for Art Libraries and Visual Resources Collections," edited by Betty Jo Irvine, was published by Libraries Unlimited for ARLIS/NA. Additionally, "World Architecture Index: a Guide to Illustrations," compiled by Edward H. Teague, was released by Greenwood Press as part of its Art Reference Collection No. 12. The Visual Resources Association (VRA) established its listserv, VRA-L, in 1992, providing a crucial communication tool for its members who are visual resources curators. In 1993, Oxford University Press published the "Users' Guide to The Art and Architecture Thesaurus" alongside the electronic edition. The VRA formed its Data Standards Committee in March 1994. Later that year, in September, Marc Andreessen left the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) to establish the Mosaic Communications Corp, which would later become Netscape. Mosaic's launch marked the beginning of the World Wide Web for the general public. Also in 1994, the first image database, SPIRO, made its debut on the World Wide Web. In 1995, the "Concordance of Ancient Site Names" was edited and published, further contributing to the growing body of work on visual resources and subject access in libraries.

The remarkable story of carrier pigeons, a breed with an innate ability to return home from great distances, has fascinated societies for centuries. These birds have been tested by being transported hundreds of miles across seas, only to find their way back with unwavering accuracy. This unique trait has proven invaluable in various human endeavors, particularly during wartime when they have been used to deliver messages across enemy lines. A notable instance involved the German Emperor, who, curious about their reliability, sent a batch of these pigeons from England to Germany. Released in Dover, they all returned to Düsseldorf within six hours, an event that sparked intrigue and concern among the English, eventually leading to a discussion in the House of Commons. In a remarkable find, a stone from Mexico's Magdalena district, located in the state of Sonora, was discovered bearing symbols remarkably akin to Chinese writing. A well-educated Chinese individual confirmed the inscription to be authentic, dating back two thousand years and suggesting a Chinese settlement in the region. This challenges the widely accepted narrative that Columbus was the first to discover the American continent, hinting at the possibility of Chinese explorers having arrived centuries earlier. Archaeological findings indicate that Chinese expeditions during the early stages of their civilization have also been identified in the Pacific Islands and Australia. King Menelik of Abyssinia's decision to appoint a Russian General as Governor-General over regions near the equator demonstrates his intention to introduce civilization to his people. M. M. de Leontieff, who had earlier traveled to Abyssinia and carried presents from the Czar, is anticipated to have a beneficial impact on the country's progress, similar to how General Gordon contributed in Egypt. The text highlights the unity of humankind, implying that distinctions between different countries are negligible, much like the varied abilities present in one household. It illustrates how environmental factors, such as climate and lifestyle, can significantly influence the physical characteristics of a population over time, as seen in the descendants of light-complexioned individuals living in tropical regions. The author posits that the human races have evolved through detachments from the original human family, each developing unique traits under local influences over thousands of years. The quest to understand the history and origins of various nations is likened to discovering long-lost relatives, prompting curiosity about their journeys and the reasons for their separation from their forebears. The author acknowledges the limitations of written records, which only extend back a few centuries, and highlights the importance of other forms of historical evidence, such as inscriptions on monuments and walls. However, the narrative also acknowledges the vast expanse of time before any form of writing existed, leaving the stories of early humans to be pieced together from fragments and interpretations.

Postmodernism is a complex and multifaceted cultural and intellectual movement that emerged in the mid-20th century. It is characterized by skepticism, relativism, and a general distrust of grand theories and ideologies. Postmodernism has had a significant impact on various fields, including music, art, literature, and philosophy. In the realm of music, postmodernism has manifested in diverse and innovative ways. Jonathan Kramer, a scholar on the subject, has observed that avant-garde compositions, which may be considered modernist by some, often challenge and extend the traditional boundaries of what constitutes music. These compositions can be provocative and unsettling, pushing the listener to reconsider their understanding of the art form. During the 1960s, a group of composers, including Terry Riley, Henryk Górecki, Bradley Joseph, John Adams, Steve Reich, Philip Glass, Michael Nyman, and Lou Harrison, sought to move away from the perceived elitism and dissonance of atonal academic modernism. They created music with simpler textures and more consonant harmonies, offering a fresh perspective on musical expression. Concurrently, artists like John Cage questioned the established notions of beauty and objectivity that were prevalent in modernism. Cage's work often incorporated unconventional sounds and methods, further expanding the definition of music. In addition to these developments in classical and avant-garde music, postmodernism has also influenced popular music genres. Dominic Strinati, an author on postmodernism, highlights the significance of "art rock" and the blending of styles seen in the works of groups like Talking Heads and performers such as Laurie Anderson. The Pet Shop Boys' self-conscious reinvention of disco is another example of postmodern musical innovation. In the late 20th century, American singer Madonna was labeled by avant-garde academics as the "personification of the postmodern." Christian writer Graham Cray and literary critic Olivier Sécardin both suggested that Madonna epitomizes postmodernism, while Martin Amis described her as "perhaps the most postmodern personage on the planet." Her ever-changing image and style, as well as her ability to reinvent herself, have made her a symbol of the postmodern era. In the field of philosophy, postmodernism arose during the 1970s as a varied and multifaceted group of scholars started to challenge and examine the prevailing narratives and beliefs of their era. These philosophers often rejected the idea of objective truth and universal values, instead advocating for a more nuanced and context-dependent understanding of knowledge and reality. Overall, postmodernism has had a profound impact on various aspects of culture and society, challenging traditional norms and encouraging a more open and questioning approach to art, music, and thought.

Hildebrand Gurlitt was a prominent German art dealer during the Nazi era. Between 1939 and 1944, he acquired numerous artworks, excluding those for his personal collection. Out of these acquisitions, 168 pieces were earmarked for the Führermuseum, a planned museum dedicated to Adolf Hitler's vision of German art. Gurlitt capitalized on his officially sanctioned buying trips to Paris, a city teeming with artworks of questionable provenance, some of which are now recognized as looted. These trips allowed him to expand his own art holdings and amass considerable wealth from commissions on the substantial sums paid by the Nazi regime for art acquisitions. In addition to his official duties, Gurlitt also purchased paintings on a personal level, particularly from artists persecuted by the Nazis. One such artist was Max Beckmann, who was living in exile in the Netherlands by 1944. Gurlitt and his associate, Erhard Göpel, the local buyer for Hitler's Führermuseum, bought five works from Beckmann in September 1944. Among these was the painting "Bar, Brown," which Gurlitt retained for himself. After Gurlitt's passing, his wife put the painting up for sale, but it did not sell. Later, his son Cornelius sold it at an auction by Ketterer in Stuttgart in 1972, where it fetched DM 90,000 after auctioneer's fees. The same painting was later resold at Sotheby's in London for £1.2 million. Beckmann's family accepted the allocation of the sale earnings without objection, viewing Gurlitt's initial acquisition as valid, even though it occurred amidst the difficult situations the artist endured. After the war, Gurlitt was captured along with his wife.

Conrad Martens (1801–1878) was a professional artist who worked from 1835 to 1878, primarily known for his landscape paintings. His artwork is recognized for its capacity to temper the landscape in accordance with European tastes. Martens' watercolour studies of Sydney Harbour are highly regarded, as they introduced Romantic ideals into his paintings. He is also noted for joining the scientist Charles Darwin on the HMS Beagle, a voyage that was also made by Augustus Earle. Between 1851 and 1885, the Victorian gold rush led to a significant influx of settlers and an increase in wealth. The artist S. T. Gill (1818–1880) recorded life on the Australian goldfields, reflecting the spirit of the time. However, the colonial art market during that period showed greater interest in landscape paintings. These were often commissioned by wealthy landowners or merchants who wanted to showcase their prosperity. One significant landscape painting from that era is "Flood in the Darling" by William Piguenit (1836–1914), which was purchased by the National Gallery of New South Wales in 1895. Other prominent artists of the time included Eugene von Guerard, Nicholas Chevalier, William Strutt, John Skinner Prout, and Knud Bull. Louis Buvelot played an important role in landscape painting during the later period. Influenced by the Barbizon school painters, Buvelot embraced a plein air method, characterized by painting outdoors to record the natural light and atmosphere. His work frequently conveyed a more domestic and tranquil perspective of the land, differing from the prior focus on unfamiliarity or peril in Australian landscape art. Buvelot's method, along with his significant impact as a teacher, has prompted some to call him the "Father of Australian landscape painting."

Otto Grashof was a German painter, illustrator, and portraitist known for his distinctive artistic contributions. Thomas Somerscales was an English seascape painter, renowned for his work such as "The Naval Battle of Iquique." In addition to these notable figures, there were several lesser-known painters of the same period whose works, though not widely celebrated, are significant. These include John Searle, María Graham, Johan Heinrich Jenny, Francis Martín Drexel, Camilo Domeniconi, Augusto Borget, Procesa del Carmen Sarmiento, Juan Bianchi, Clara Filleul, Alexander Simón, Giovatto Molinelli, and Theodor Ohlsen. The Chilean Precursors of Chilean painting were a group of artists who, similar to their foreign contemporaries based in Chile, were influenced by European art. These Chilean painters did not follow a unified style but operated concurrently and were instrumental in initiating a new phase of Chilean art through the founding of the Chilean Academy of Painting. Galaz and Ivaelic observed that the works of these artists were deeply linked to the Chilean landscape, its people, and cultural aspects. Among the Chilean painters who were part of this movement, Manuel Antonio Caro stands out as the most remarkable artist of this period. His style was realistic, often depicting customs and folkloric scenes. Some of his most famous paintings include "La Zamacueca" and "The Abdication of O’Higgins." Caro also became a member of the newly founded academy. Francisco Javier Mandiola was another prominent figure in this movement, known for portraying local customs and considered the most talented pupil of Raymond. His work contributed to the rich tapestry of Chilean art during this period, showcasing the diverse cultural and social aspects of the country.

In his essay on gardening, Horace Walpole touches upon a concept that epitomizes a fundamental principle: the modern style of gardening emerged from the invention of the "ha-ha" by Bridgeman, a pioneer in landscape gardening. The "ha-ha" allowed a garden to blend harmoniously with the surrounding countryside, separated only by an invisible barrier rather than a wall. This concept challenges the notion that a garden lover would prefer nature to art, as a garden is, in essence, an artistic creation that replaces the untamed wilderness. The affection for nature, as demonstrated by later individuals such as Lord Byron, may at times approach misanthropy, valuing the wild for its intrinsic worth. However, the landscape gardener believes that their art should be subordinate to nature, incorporating the wider scenery into their designs rather than excluding it. This viewpoint echoes the beliefs of Telford, who considered rivers to exist for the benefit of canals, and Gilpin, who assessed nature through the lens of the "theory of the picturesque." Gilpin observed that although nature's arrangements might appear cold and individualistic, they do not fall into "mannerism." Put differently, nature functions as a sublime landscape artist whose creations must be acknowledged and integrated by the human gardener. An interesting example of this theory can be found in a lecture delivered by Henry Tilney in Jane Austen's "Mansfield Park." According to Walpole's theory, the development of the "ha-ha" symbolizes a growing alliance between man and nature, the landowner and the countryside. This alliance is characterized by improved roads and inns, the gradual integration of urban and rural areas, and a growing awareness of the drawbacks of overpopulated cities. The love for nature has deep roots, with poets from Chaucer onwards celebrating the beauty of landscapes, the arrival of spring, and the splendors of storms and sunsets. The indifference to nature displayed by the Pope school was a temporary phenomenon, reflecting the self-assuredness of the urban population and their disdain for the rustic outside world. However, the love for field sports remained strong among the squire class, and as they began to receive intellectual influences from the city, they started to express emotions that found clear expression in works like Izaak Walton's "The Compleat Angler." The old poets often used nature as a backdrop for human action, focusing on concrete facts and the joys of sports or rustic amusements. They adhered to old conventions and engaged in conversations with imaginary shepherds, Robin Hood, or allegorical knights in romantic forests. In contrast, during Pope's time, nature emerged as an abstract or metaphysical deity that could be worshipped with a distinct appreciation. Pope himself, influenced by Bolingbroke and Shaftesbury, expounded on the stars and the animal world in his "Essay on Man." Shaftesbury, in particular, emphasized the aesthetic perspective of nature, asserting that the Good, the True, and the Beautiful are all one, and that the universe impresses us as an artistic embodiment of harmony. This perspective led to a legitimate development of the love for beauty, as seen in works like Akenside's "The Pleasures of Imagination" and Henry Brooke's "Universal Beauty." James Thomson's "The Seasons," with its fine "Hymn of Nature," represents this current of sentiment. Thomson's descriptions of nature, intended to serve as a sermon, show a growing interest in country life and a challenge to the supremacy of the urban wit. However, Thomson's philosophy and observation remain somewhat separate, and his masterpiece, the didactic poem on "Liberty," remains largely forgotten. In conclusion, the love for nature has evolved over time, from being a backdrop for human action to becoming an object of admiration and worship in its own right. The landscape gardener's approach to subordinating art to nature and incorporating the wider scenery into their designs reflects a growing appreciation for the beauty and harmony of the natural world.

He was a jay, indeed, and I had just witnessed his rather cad-like behavior towards Mrs. Bevidge," one character remarked. "Then I'm at a loss as to why you were in his company," another responded. "Oh, you do understand, Alan. You mustn't apply logic here! It's like questioning how you became more serious than sober." The brother laughed, unable to argue. "It was the excitement," he explained. "But you can't indulge in such behavior, Bess," he chided, his tone heavy with the weight of his own past mistakes. "I know I shouldn't, but I do," she retorted. "I understand it's detrimental to me, if not to others. Let's make a pact to stop!" "I'm always ready to make such a promise," the young man agreed, his voice tinged with melancholy. He added, "But you have a sharp mind, Bess, and I dislike seeing you act foolishly." "Do you truly, Alan?" the girl inquired, seemingly pleased by his criticism as much as his compliment. "Do you think I have a sharp mind?" "You're the only girl who does," he affirmed. "Oh, I didn't mean to ask for that much! But why can't I utilize it effectively? Other girls draw, play music, write. I only seek the excitement that's bad for me. I wish you could explain it." Alan Lynde did not attempt to answer. The question seemed to redirect his thoughts inward, causing him to feel disheartened. "I possess a sharp mind too, I believe," he began. "Lots of them!" his sister interjected, generously. "There's no man who can compare to you. If I could talk with you all the time, I wouldn't need the company of jays. I'm not flattering you. You're always a feast of reason; I have no interest in emotional outpourings. You always take the right view of things when you're being yourself, and even when you're not, you're not stupid. You could be anything you chose." "The problem is that I can't choose," he replied. "Yes, I suppose that is the problem," she agreed. "You shouldn't use such language, Bess," her brother admonished, sternly. "Oh, I don't with everyone," she defended herself. "Never with ladies!" He glanced at her with a smile that was both rueful and humorous. "You got me, I guess," he admitted. "'Touché,' Mr. Durgin says. He fences and speaks French. It's as if an animal were speaking French; you're always anticipating them to speak English. But I don't mind your swearing in my presence; I know it helps to dissipate the tension." She laughed, and coaxed a laugh from him as well. "Is there anything to him?" he asked, once their laughter subsided. "Yes, quite a bit," Bessie replied thoughtfully, and then she went on to recount all that Jeff had told her about himself, describing his composure in dealing with the benevolent Mrs. Bevidge, as she referred to her, and sketching his character as she perceived it. Her sketch was filled with astute conjectures and she made it entertaining for her brother, who, from his own perspective of mischief, undoubtedly judged the original more intelligently. "Well, you'd better avoid him after this," he advised at the end. "Yes," she agreed pensively. "I suppose it's like developing a taste for a very common type of whiskey, isn't it? I see what you mean. If one must indulge, it should be in champagne." She turned to him with a look of keen yet limited understanding, which always makes women's conjectures about vice so amusing or so touching to men. "Better avoid the champagne as well," her brother suggested darkly. "Yes, I know," she conceded, sinking back into her chair and staring dreamily at the fire. After a while, she asked abruptly, "Will you stop if I will?" "I'm afraid I couldn't," he replied. "You could try," she encouraged. "Oh, I'm used to it," he said. "Then it's a deal," she declared, jumping from her chair and going over to him. She smoothed his hair over his forehead and kissed the spot she had smoothed, despite its unpleasant dampness to her lips. "Poor boy, poor boy! Now, remember! No more jays for me, and no more sprees for you. Goodnight." Jeff Durgin was uncertain whether Miss Bessie Lynde intended to attend Mrs. Bevidge's Thursday gatherings or not.

The "Foundations and Futures" symposium was a significant gathering held in Columbus, Indiana, which included a fully booked keynote presentation with well-known speakers like Deborah Berke, Will Miller, Robert A. M. Stern, and Michael Van Valkenburgh. M. Stern, and Michael Van Valkenburgh. The symposium also included sessions with experts on various topics, including the history of modern architecture, the unique aspects of Columbus, Indiana, fabrication techniques, and community engagement. This event was promoted as the inaugural step towards launching an exhibition, which was scheduled for August 2017. All ten of the 2016 Miller Prize Finalists had the chance to take part in panel discussions, enhancing the symposium's comprehensive content. The 2016 symposium was recognized by NUVO as a "2016 Best Of Editors Pick," underscoring its importance within the field. Project Development: The initial planning for Exhibit Columbus began in late 2014, and the project was formally inaugurated on May 5, 2016, in Columbus as an initiative of Heritage Fund—The Community Foundation of Bartholomew County. The initiative is supported by funding from various local and regional individuals, foundations, and corporations, ensuring its sustainability and growth. 100 Variations Exhibition: In the fall of 2014, a pilot project known as "100 Variations" was developed.
