The exhibition was produced by Indianapolis-based curator Christopher West, with support from the Haddad Foundation, the Columbus Area Visitors Center, and the Columbus Museum of Art and Design. Each table was crafted by Noblitt Fabricating in Columbus, Indiana, under the direction of Curt Aton. Graphic Identity: In 2016, the Chicago-based graphic design firm Thirst was commissioned to develop the graphic identity for the Exhibit Columbus. Their work played a crucial role in establishing a cohesive and recognizable visual representation for the project, enhancing its overall impact and appeal.

The idea of maintaining neutrality, referred to as [Greek: epochê], represents a condition that results in a feeling of calmness termed [Greek: ataraxia]. Pyrrho, a philosopher whose questions were posed in a manner reminiscent of Kant, sought not to develop a system of truth but to explore the nature of philosophy itself. His dedication to this pursuit is illustrated by an anecdote from Diogenes, in which Pyrrho was found talking to himself, contemplating how to become a virtuous person ([Greek: chrêstos]). This story reveals a depth of character distinct from the typical skepticism found in Sextus' works. The essence of Pyrrho's philosophy and his approach to life can be largely attributed to his personal disposition. His indifference was inherent to his calm nature and was not solely a product of his philosophical beliefs. While this attitude could be aspired to, it could never be fully replicated. One of his followers noted that to truly embrace Pyrrho's teachings, one must possess a similar temperament. Diogenes records that Pyrrho was the first to propose the rudimentary principles of skepticism, although his ideas were not yet fully developed, as he left no written works. There is no evidence of Pyrrho formulating the Tropes, but it is likely that he recognized some contradictions in sensory experiences, possibly hinting at the Tropes in a nascent form. Among the many skeptical maxims, or [Greek: phônai], the three that are most closely associated with the origins of skepticism are the [Greek: antilogia], the [Greek: ouden horizô], and the [Greek: ou mallon]. Diogenes cites Protagoras as the source for the idea that there are always two opposing arguments for everything. The phrase "to determine nothing" is attributed to Timon's _Python_, and the other two maxims are also linked to him by Aristocles. The [Greek: ou mallon] is directly associated with Democritus, though Pyrrho's interpretation of this phrase may have differed, as noted by Sextus. It is probable that Pyrrho employed all three of these sayings, as suggested by Diogenes. However, this led to accusations from the Dogmatics that the Skeptics were dogmatizing simply by possessing such sayings. Sextus refuted this by arguing that these maxims also encompass their own meaning, similar to how a purgative removes itself along with other harmful substances. In comparing the later Pyrrhonism with the teachings of Pyrrho, there is a stark contrast in the moral stance of the two. For Pyrrho, the equilibrium of the soul was a means to apply to his positive theory of life, whereas for the later Pyrrhoneans, it was the ultimate goal. However, the empirical tendency that characterized the history of Pyrrhonism can be traced back to Pyrrho as its originator. He was an empirical philosopher, and his influence in this regard was in stark contrast to the dialectical spirit of Academic Skepticism. The empiricism of the school is evident in its scientific knowledge, the fact that many Skeptics were physicians, and in the nature of the ten Tropes of [Greek: epochê]. It is safe to assert that the foundational principles of Pyrrhonism are attributable to Pyrrho and his originality, which gave the school its strength. However, the more elaborate arguments and the specifics of its maxims belong to later periods. Regarding the relationship between Pyrrhonism and the Academy, the connection is challenging to pinpoint with precision, especially between the time of Pyrrho and Aenesidemus. However, skepticism within the Academy was never entirely the same as Pyrrhonism, even though there were periods in the history of the Academy when the difference was minimal. Arcesilaus, who brought doubt into the Academy, sought to revert to the dialectic of Socrates. He replaced lectures with discussions, which he believed to be a more Socratic method of teaching. Despite Sextus' assertion that Arcesilaus' skepticism was the closest to Pyrrhonism, his teachings were fundamentally rooted in the dialectical principle, which was in opposition to the empiricism of Pyrrho. The belief in the existence of absolute truth, as held by Socrates and Plato, never completely lost its influence over the Academy. This belief eventually led the Academy back to Dogmatism and paved the way for the Eclecticism that marked its departure from history. The histories of Pyrrhonism and Academic Skepticism were contemporaneous for some time. Timon, the immediate follower of Pyrrho and referred to by Sextus as the "prophet of Pyrrho," was a contemporary of Arcesilaus. His decision not to become part of the Academy and his works suggest that he did not consider the Academy's skepticism equivalent to Pyrrhonism.

Hans Melzian, a scholar, has contributed significantly to the understanding of the Bini language, which is predominantly spoken in Southern Nigeria. His work, "A Concise Dictionary of the Bini Language," is a valuable resource for those interested in this linguistic field. The dictionary is available for free download, borrowing, and streaming through the Internet Archive. In addition to Melzian's work, another important document related to the region is the autobiography of Jacob Egharevba, titled "ITAN ẸDAGBỌN MWEN." This autobiography is written in the Edo language, which is another significant language in Nigeria. The Edo language is spoken by the Edo people, who primarily reside in the Edo State of Nigeria. Both of these works provide valuable insights into the languages and cultures of Southern Nigeria, offering readers a deeper understanding of the linguistic diversity in the region. The availability of these resources online allows for a wider audience to access and appreciate the rich linguistic heritage of Nigeria.

The article examines the debate about the death of Seth Rich, a Democratic National Committee (DNC) employee, along with the following media attention. Rod Wheeler, a private investigator, was hired by Rodger Stone and a wealthy Trump supporter, Ed Butowsky, to investigate Rich's murder. There were claims that Rich had leaked DNC emails to WikiLeaks, but these allegations have been largely debunked. In May 2017, Fox News published a story suggesting a link between Rich and the FBI, which was later retracted. The story was based on Wheeler's investigation, but he later claimed that quotes attributed to him were fabricated. Wheeler sued Fox News for defamation, alleging that the network had manipulated his claims. The lawsuit was dismissed in August 2018, with the judge ruling that there was no evidence of manipulation. Butowsky also faced a lawsuit from the Rich family, who accused him of exploiting their son's death for political purposes. The lawsuit was dismissed for similar reasons as Wheeler's, with the judge finding no evidence of wrongdoing on Butowsky's part. It is important to note that the claims of a connection between Rich, the DNC, and WikiLeaks have been widely discredited by multiple investigations, including those conducted by the U.S. intelligence community. The consensus among experts is that Russia was responsible for the hacking of the DNC's computer systems and the subsequent release of emails. In conclusion, the Seth Rich story has been a source of much controversy and misinformation. While some individuals have sought to use the incident to advance their political agendas, the evidence overwhelmingly points to Russia as the culprit behind the DNC hacking. It is crucial for the public to critically evaluate the information presented in the media and to rely on credible sources for accurate news.

Suppose a President were elected on the promise of expanding military forces immediately following a European war. To consider the potential consequences further would be an insult to our intelligence. The establishment of "defensive" alliances, whether directed against or in support of us—if we could somehow convince others to participate—would result in increasing tensions, acts of provocation, and a reoccurrence of previous historical conflicts. However, should such a devastating war take place, it would not be a misfortune if we had brought it upon ourselves. The real tragedy would be if we lacked the intrinsic value that Germany possesses to justify our actions. The true sorrow would be that we were so preoccupied with the faults of others that we neglected to address our own shortcomings. I Am Woman Marguerite Swawite I am woman: as ancient as the Lebanon cedars and even older; as youthful as the newest green shoot that emerges through the snow in March. My face is turned to the East, flushed with the dawn of my potential; my hands are restrained by the binding touch of the solitary woman who, driven by desire, knew only the need for a kiss on her throat and a child in the curve of her arm. Today, I am a woman, somewhat diminished yet a bit more so; for I am discovering how to sing not his tune, nor someone else's, but my own, which has resided in my heart since the very first day. It will be a magnificent golden melody, though not always soft with a sweet rhythm, for I must strive to sing. I am learning to sustain myself on nothing, yet remain fulfilled; to warm my cold limbs without fire; to continue my journey without a kiss or a child, even though my lips are red and my arms willing. Yet, I know I will never cease until I have sung it all—every last note. Even in the distant days to come, as they beckon to me in the rosy dawn, I will still be woman. My song will become sweetly familiar, and he who was once frightened will draw near, singing his separate song, always his own, yet blending its masculine tones with mine. Together, we will create a grand harmony that envelops the world in our music, rejoicing once more in our union. That day will come... But today, I am weary—the East is rosy with the promise of dawn. (The following is one of the poems in Edgar Lee Master’s “Spoon River Anthology” which has been featured in Reedy’s St. Louis Mirror and has garnered widespread attention. In our opinion, it is among the finest poetry.) Caroline Branson With our hearts like drifting suns, had we only walked as often before the April fields until starlight softened the darkness under the rock, our trysting place in the wood, where the brook turns! Had we only transitioned from courtship like notes of music that merge, into the inspired improvisation of love! But to leave behind the enchantment of the flesh, in which our souls swooned, descending into a realm where time, space, and our individual selves ceased to exist—annihilated in love! To abandon these experiences for a room with lamps; to stand with our secret mocking itself, hiding among flowers and mandolins, observed by all between salad and coffee. To witness his trembling and feel my own premonition, as if signing a bond—not ablaze with gifts and pledges heaped with rosy hands over his brow. And then, O night! Deliberate! Unlovely! With all our courtship wiped away by the act of love in a selected room at a time known to everyone. The next day, he sat so listless, almost cold, so strangely changed, wondering why I wept, until a kind of sick despair and voluptuous madness seized us, leading us to make the pact of death. A stalk of the earth sphere, fragile as starlight, awaits being drawn once again into creation's stream. But next time, to be born under the gaze of Raphael and St. Francis, as they pass by. For I am their younger sibling, to be unmistakably recognized in a future cycle of birth. You may know the seed and the soil; you may feel the cold rain fall. But only the earth-sphere and heaven know the secret of the seed in the nuptial chamber under the soil. Throw me into the stream again, give me another trial—Save me, Shelley! Music The Kneisel Quartet and Hofmannized Chopin Albert Spalding What more fortunate combination could be desired than this: Albert Spalding performing the Mendelssohn Violin Concerto with the Thomas Orchestra! On two occasions, four thousand people were warmed to genuine enthusiasm; and at both the Friday and Saturday concerts, the orchestra members (whose typically bored demeanor is their usual tribute) were roused and showed the strongest appreciation for the young man's artistry. Frederick Stock beamed, fatherly, as he clapped his hands.

The Phoenician civilization, known for its maritime prowess and trade networks, has long been a subject of fascination and speculation regarding its influence on other cultures. One such debate revolves around the possibility of Phoenician contact with ancient American civilizations. However, the evidence supporting this theory is limited and often disputed. The Phoenicians are credited with developing an early form of the alphabet, which has influenced the writing systems used across Europe and Southwestern Asia today. This script differs from the writing systems present in ancient American civilizations, including those at Palenque and Copan. The inscriptions in these American sites bear no resemblance to Phoenician writing, nor do they share any characteristics with the Phoenician language or architectural styles. In 1872, a stone purportedly inscribed with Phoenician script was discovered in Paraíba, Brazil. The inscription allegedly told the story of a Phoenician ship that was separated from a fleet sailing from Egypt around Africa during a storm. It also mentioned a pharaoh, either Necho I or Necho II. The stone was initially accepted as genuine by Ladislau de Souza Mello Netto, the director of the National Museum of Brazil. However, by 1873, the philologist Ernest Renan had persuaded Netto that the inscription was a forgery, due to the differences in letter forms compared to those used by the Phoenicians. The lack of a common linguistic or scriptural heritage between the Phoenicians and ancient American civilizations, along with the questionable authenticity of the Paraíba stone, makes it difficult to establish a concrete connection between these two cultures. Although the notion of Phoenician impact on American civilizations is compelling, the existing evidence fails to substantiate this hypothesis. Further research and discovery may shed more light on this topic in the future, but for now, the relationship between the Phoenicians and ancient American cultures remains speculative.

Christianity posits that it is possible to discern the existence of God, while atheism asserts the opposite, claiming that there is no God. Agnosticism, on the other hand, maintains a neutral stance, arguing that there is insufficient evidence to definitively confirm or deny the existence of a higher power. In an essay, the philosopher Bertrand Russell suggests that extraordinary personal experiences, such as hearing a voice from the sky predicting specific events that later transpire, could potentially sway one's belief towards the existence of a superhuman intelligence. Leslie Weatherhead, a Christian theologian (1893–1976), presented a refined viewpoint on agnosticism in his 1965 book, "The Christian Agnostic." He argued that numerous individuals who identify as agnostics might possess a more accurate comprehension of God compared to some frequent attendees of churches who might have incorrect notions regarding the divine. Although Weatherhead's views were considered radical and unpalatable by traditional theologians, his form of agnosticism is less extreme than that of Thomas Huxley, often referred to as "Darwin's Bulldog." Weatherhead believed in the human soul's inherent capacity to reject or accept God, given the essential nature of choice, but he was convinced that ultimately, no one would choose to reject the divine. In the United States, Robert G. Ingersoll (1833–1899), an Illinois lawyer, politician, and celebrated orator of the 19th century, was known as "The Great Agnostic." His skepticism and thorough analysis of religious doctrines, especially during an 1896 speech, helped establish him as a key figure within the agnostic movement.

Mersenne, a prominent philosopher and scientist of the 17th century, believed in the formulation of laws and rules for sense-perceptions through scientific inquiry. He argued against the idea of doubting everything by highlighting several points: 1. Humans have common agreements on certain facts, such as the fact that an ant is smaller than an elephant. 2. Natural laws, like those of optics, regulate our sensory experiences and assist in correcting errors. 3. Human-made instruments such as rulers and scales are employed to measure and dispel uncertainties regarding occurrences like curved oars, pigeons' necks, and circular towers. However, a Pyrrhonist might counter these arguments by stating that senses can deceive, leading to infinite regress or circular logic. Mersenne countered this by claiming that widely accepted principles can be proposed and examined through time to confirm their accuracy. He also pointed out that if everything can be doubted, then doubt itself can be doubted, implying that some level of certainty is necessary. Mersenne believed that mathematical, physical, and other scientific knowledge, which has been tested repeatedly, holds true and has practical value. He was one of the few philosophers who accepted Thomas Hobbes' radical ideology, considering it a new science of man. Thomas Hobbes (1588-1679) was actively involved in the circle of major skeptics like Gassendi and Mersenne during his long stay in Paris. While Hobbes shared the interest in skepticism and epistemology with his fellow skeptics, he held a unique perspective compared to them.

The Renaissance period in Europe saw the rise of a major intellectual movement known as Renaissance Humanism. It was characterized by a renewed interest in the study of classical antiquity, particularly the literature, philosophy, and art of ancient Greece and Rome. This movement sought to revive the values and knowledge of the ancient world and apply them to contemporary society. One of the key figures in the development of Renaissance Humanism was Lovato Lovato, an Italian poet and scholar. He was followed by other prominent humanists such as Leonardo Bruni, who further advanced the movement. The origins and evolution of humanism during this period have been extensively studied and documented by scholars like Ronald Witt in his work "In the Footsteps of the Ancients: The Origins of Humanism from Lovato to Bruni," published by Brill Publishers in 2000. Another important aspect of Renaissance Humanism was the influence of paganism. Edgar Wind's book "Pagan Mysteries in the Renaissance," released by W.W. Norton in 1969, examines how pagan beliefs and practices contributed to the cultural and intellectual environment of the Renaissance. This book provides valuable insights into the complex relationship between Christianity and paganism during this period. Charles, in "The Scope of Renaissance Humanism," published by the University of Michigan Press in 1983, offers a comprehensive analysis of the movement, its impact on various aspects of society, and the key figures who contributed to its development. For those interested in learning more about Renaissance Humanism, there are several external resources available. The World History Encyclopedia offers a general summary of the subject, whereas Albert Rabil Jr.'s "Humanism 1: An Outline" presents a brief introduction to the topic. Additionally, the Library of Congress's article "Rome Reborn: The Vatican Library & Renaissance Culture: Humanism," published on July 1, 2002, discusses the role of the Vatican Library in the preservation and dissemination of humanist ideas. Furthermore, the BBC Radio 4 program "In Our Time" featured a discussion on "Paganism in the Renaissance" with Tom Healy, Charles Hope, and Evelyn Welch on June 16, 2005. This discussion provides an engaging and informative perspective on the influence of paganism during the Renaissance period. In summary, Renaissance Humanism was a crucial intellectual movement that sought to revive and apply the knowledge and values of classical antiquity to the contemporary world. The study of this movement offers a deeper understanding of the cultural and intellectual transformations that took place during the Renaissance.

The Ministry of Love in George Orwell's dystopian novel "Nineteen Eighty-Four" serves a crucial purpose. It is tasked with the "rehabilitation" of thought criminals, who are subsequently released as devoted subjects conditioned to worship Big Brother, thereby fulfilling the name of the Ministry. In different film versions of the novel, the portrayal of Big Brother's character has varied. In the 1954 BBC version, production designer Roy Oxley was shown through a single still image. The 1956 film adaptation depicted Big Brother as a stern-looking disembodied head illustration. In the 1984 film starring John Hurt, the photograph of Big Brother was that of actor Bob Flag. Both Flag and Oxley were shown with tiny mustaches. Since the publication of "Nineteen Eighty-Four," the term "Big Brother" has become a common metaphor for any intrusive or overly controlling authority figure, as well as for government surveillance efforts. The idea of Big Brother and other Orwellian symbols are frequently invoked in the joke referred to as the Russian reversal. In their 1956 book "Blood Royal," Iain Moncreiffe and Don Pottinger humorously mentioned the sentence: "Without Little Father, no need for Big Brother," alluding to the Russian Revolution and the Soviet Union. The global reality television series "Big Brother" draws its concept from the novel's idea of perpetual monitoring. In 2000, following the debut of the U.S. edition of the CBS show "Big Brother," the Estate of George Orwell initiated legal action against CBS and its production firm, Orwell Productions, Inc., in a federal court located in Chicago.

"Living by the Sword" is a phrase that has been used in various contexts to convey the idea that those who rely on violence or aggression will ultimately be affected by it themselves. This concept can be traced back to historical and religious texts, suggesting that the use of force tends to perpetuate a cycle of violence. In popular culture, the phrase has been referenced in music. For instance, in Megadeth's song "Five Magics," frontman Dave Mustaine includes the line "He who lives by the sword, will surely also die," which echoes the sentiment of the proverb. Similarly, in Bob Seger's "Night Moves," the third verse features the phrase "Living by the Sword," thereby highlighting the phrase's broader cultural significance. The concept of living by the sword is often contrasted with the idea of Christian pacifism, which promotes nonviolence and peaceful conflict resolution. The phrase "beat swords into ploughshares" is also related, as it suggests the transformation of weapons into tools for peaceful purposes, symbolizing the shift from a violent to a peaceful society. While the phrase "living by the sword" has been used to discuss the consequences of a violent lifestyle, it is important to note that the interpretation and application of this concept can vary depending on the context in which it is used. As such, readers are encouraged to explore various perspectives and sources to form their own understanding of the phrase and its implications.

In the Scholastic philosophical tradition, the idea of the soul plays a key role in comprehending the nature of living entities. According to Thomas Aquinas and other Thomists, beings of the same genus share an essence, differing only in accidents and substantial form. The soul is defined as the substantial form of living beings, distinguishing them from one another. Plants possess what is known as "vegetative souls," which are responsible for their growth and development. Animals, on the other hand, are endowed with "sensitive souls," granting them the ability to perceive and react to their environment. Human beings are unique in that they possess "intellectual souls," which are characterized by rationality and immortality. Aristotle's perspective on the soul is one of unity, with the soul being a single entity endowed with five distinct groups of faculties, or "dunámeis." These faculties are: 1. The "vegetative" faculty (threptikón), which is concerned with the maintenance and development of organic life. 2. The appetite (oretikón), representing the tendency to seek out what is perceived as good. 3. The faculty of sense perception (aisthetikón), enabling the perception of the external world. 4. The "locomotive" faculty (kinetikón), which governs bodily movements. 5. Reason (dianoetikón), the highest faculty, associated with intellectual and rational thought. Scholastic philosophers generally follow Aristotle's classification, viewing the body and soul as a unified whole. The soul is considered the "forma substantialis," or the vital principle, that serves as the source of all activities. As a result, the study of the soul encompasses functions that are now typically associated with biology and physiology. The relationship between the mind and the organism is a matter of philosophical or metaphysical inquiry. In terms of human appetite, it is divided into two parts: the rational and the irrational. The rational aspect is known as the will, while the irrational aspect is referred to as passion. In the realm of ethics, Thomas Aquinas agrees with Aristotle's definition of happiness as "an operation according to perfect virtue." He further asserts that happiness is a state that is uniquely human, as it is achieved through the exercise of virtue. This perspective emphasizes the importance of moral and intellectual development in achieving a fulfilling and meaningful life.

"Very well, then," came the response, "but in exchange for my silence, you must inquire whether Kate has sewn the tassel on my smoking-cap as she promised." "Of course I did," a cheerful voice replied. Kate emerged from the parlor, the cap in her hand, looking lovelier than ever. "Ah, thank you, dear Kate! Now make sure to keep Paul in good spirits while I go to enjoy my cigar. It would be impolite to leave him by himself." Kate smiled, and their intended walk on the piazza was substituted with a stroll down the avenue. It must have been a pleasant stroll, as when the tea bell rang, they were still there, observing the pale moon rise, and pondering to themselves how often they would experience such moments with the same joy. They didn't wonder for long. Each evening, Paul Linden would challenge someone to a walk, and somehow, everyone was tired except Kate, and everyone was busy except Kate. It wasn't long before the whispering leaves bore witness to a pledge of love between the two, and heard (if leaves could hear) what Paul Linden considered the softest music on earth—the low tones that conveyed to him the surrender of sweet Kate de la Croix's heart. The leaves saw a strange ring gleaming on her fair hand, and they remained discreet—but not the sisters. Minnie noticed the tiny emblem representing their shared belief, and unfortunate Kate shared her secret with her while crying and weeping. Even though she was unhappy that night, she remembered the burst of sorrow that came after the secret was revealed, and another bird flew from the nest just about as soon as the wedding ended. Mr. de la Croix smoked an unusually large number of cigars that evening when his daughter departed, and the sisters tried to remain cheerful; but none of them went to bed without entering Kate's empty room to weep anew. Lisa had to threaten to turn it into a storage room for rags before they could get used to passing by without entering and mourning her absence as if she would never return. "Don't keep grieving over Kate," she would say; "she will come back, and you should hold off on being happy until then." "But we miss her so very much, Lisa," said Rose, her eyes full of tears. "So do I, but you don't see me crying over an old glove or a scrap of writing like you do. And you can't say that I love her any less than the rest of her sisters." "Moreover, my dear girls," said Kenneth, taking his seat among them and lifting little Ernest onto his knee, "your spirits affect your father's. He feels the loss of his child, and you must all try to talk about her return, not her departure. I know how much you feel Kate's absence, but you must start looking at your separation as something that will happen one day. It is inherent in nature. There are three more who need to leave their home; how can you expect that all can be as fortunate as Blanche and Kate, who stay with you as before? Paul's business will likely keep him away for a year, but he will return to settle here with us, and we must look at the bright side of things as long as we can. I have been telling all this to Blanche, who ought to be just as sensible as Lisa; and now I am here to beg you, for your own good, to bear unavoidable hardships with the courage that becomes so valuable after you attain it. Minnie needs a scolding, I'm afraid," he continued, stroking her head affectionately. "Why don't you play the piano and sing as usual? The sound of music will lift our spirits, and the mechanical exercise of those little fingers will occupy your mind after a while, especially if you start working on those études by Moschelles, whose difficulty I have heard so much about." He smiled so encouragingly that Minnie hurried off to follow his advice, and soon after, Mr. de la Croix came out of his room, saying he was glad to hear the piano playing again. Minnie was fully rewarded when she saw him take his old seat and doze while she played; and she told Kenneth in confidence that she was grateful for the scolding, but he must not tell Lisa, because she might take advantage of it. That night, a long letter from Kate arrived, which helped to comfort them all. Poor Kate! Her return was destined to be a sorrowful one, for on the journey, her beautiful little girl, her darling Blanche, fell ill and declined so rapidly that by the time she reached home, there was no hope left. Silently, they cradled her in their arms and carried her to her own room, laying the little sufferer on the bed.

At that time, Fra Giovanni Agnolo, who was later appointed a Cardinal by Pope Paul III, felt a deep sense of gratitude towards Angelo, the General at Arezzo. Angelo had raised him and instilled in him a love for literature. In recognition of Angelo's influence, Agnolo crafted a stunning grey sandstone tomb for him in S. Piero, Arezzo. The tomb included detailed carvings, a realistic depiction of General Angelo on the sarcophagus, and two full-sized figures of mourning children representing the end of life's flame. Despite the tomb not being fully completed, Agnolo was summoned to Florence to assist with the city's festive preparations for the Emperor Charles V's victorious return from Tunis. Upon his arrival in Florence, Agnolo created an impressive eight-braccia figure of the River Arno on the Ponte a S. Trinita. The figure seemed to celebrate the Emperor's arrival alongside other rivers represented by statues crafted by other artists. Agnolo also created a twelve-braccia high figure of Jason, the leader of the Argonauts, on the Canto de' Carnesecchi. However, due to the large size and limited time, this work did not achieve the perfection of the Arno figure. Similarly, the figure of August Gladness he made on the Canto alla Cuculia did not meet the same acclaim. Although the period was brief, Agnolo's creations brought him significant recognition and reputation among artisans and the general public. After completing his work in Arezzo, Agnolo learned that Girolamo Genga had a marble project in Urbino. However, when the talks did not succeed, Agnolo went to Rome and subsequently to Naples, aiming to construct the tomb for the respected poet, Jacopo Sannazzaro. Sannazzaro had built a beautiful residence at Margoglino, which he bequeathed to the Order of Servite Friars upon his death. He instructed his executors, Signor Cesare Mormerio and the Lord Count d'Aliffe, to build his tomb in the church he had built. The friars proposed Agnolo for the task, and after receiving a significant portion of the payment, he commissioned Francesco del Tadda of Fiesole to assist with the project. While preparing for the tomb, Agnolo was approached by four influential men appointed to fortify Naples against the advancing Turkish army. However, Agnolo, believing it inappropriate for a man of religion to engage in war-related work, informed the executors that he would complete the project either in Carrara or Florence. Agnolo then traveled to Florence, where he was commissioned by Signora Donna Maria, the mother of Duke Cosimo, to finish the S. Cosimo for the tomb of Lorenzo de' Medici. He also created a model for a Hercules statue to be placed atop a fountain at the Duke's villa at Castello. The model was favorably received, and Agnolo was told to extract the marble from Carrara. While in Carrara, Agnolo received a letter from Cardinal Doria, who sought a sculptor to complete a statue of Prince Doria, initially assigned to Bandinelli. Despite Cardinal Cibo's efforts to send Agnolo to Genoa, Agnolo insisted on fulfilling his commitment to Duke Cosimo first. At this time, he achieved considerable advancement in the construction of Sannazzaro's tomb and the Hercules statue. Upon returning to Florence, Agnolo worked diligently on the Hercules statue. However, rumors circulated that the marble was not as perfect as the model, and Agnolo faced difficulties fitting the legs to the torso. Messer Pier Francesco Riccio, the majordomo, began to withhold payments, influenced by Bandinelli's animosity towards Agnolo and the support of Tribolo, who was working on the Castello's ornaments. Feeling mistreated, Agnolo left for Genoa, where he received the commission for the statue of Prince Doria from Cardinal Doria and the Prince. He finished the statue while continuing to supervise the work on Sannazzaro's tomb. The statue was well-received in Genoa, but Agnolo was disappointed when it was placed on the Piazza della Signoria instead of the Piazza Doria, as he had designed it to stand alone on a pedestal. In summary, where an artwork is positioned significantly affects its appearance, since the artist takes into account illumination and perspectives while creating it.

The Catholic University of Taiwan is renowned for establishing the first graduate institute of philosophy in the region. The university's newly adopted motto, "Truth, Goodness, Beauty, Sanctity," reflects its dedication to promoting intellectual advancement and philosophical exploration. This vision was instrumental in the development of the Fu Jen Philosophy Department, which emerged as a leading center for Scholasticism in Taiwan. The department's prominence was largely due to the influential philosophical theories of Yu Pin, particularly his concept of the "Three Kinds of Knowing" (三知論). Over the six decades following World War II, the university's philosophical endeavors evolved into a unique school of thought, deeply rooted in the rich history of Christian philosophy. The scholarly efforts of Fu Jen Catholic University's academics have come to be known as the "Chinese Neo Scholastic Philosophy" group. This intellectual movement has been recognized as the "Fu Jen School," reflecting the university's lasting impact on philosophical studies. Notable members of this group include Bernard Li, Gabriel Chen, Ying Ly, Chien-ming Chu, and Hsiao Chih Sun. The university's scholarly contributions are further showcased through its publication, "Universitas: Monthly Review of Philosophy and Culture," which is indexed in the Arts & Humanities Citation Index (A&HCI). Fu Jen Religious Studies is another significant area of research within the institution. For further exploration of related topics, one may refer to the Kyoto School, a Japanese intellectual movement that shares some philosophical similarities with the Fu Jen School. Additional resources and external links can provide a deeper understanding of Scholasticism and the philosophical traditions that have shaped the academic landscape at Fu Jen Catholic University.

During the 1980s, a surge of culturally and creatively progressive individuals emerged, proposing innovative ideas that contributed to the development of an alternative lifestyle. Larry Butler was a prominent figure among these visionaries. He was employed as a caretaker at the Diorama, the first cinematic house in London, located in Regent's Park. Butler was both a committed caretaker and a trailblazer in communication, recognized for his brilliance and forward-thinking guidance. The Diorama building became a hub for artists and performers in the late 1970s. They adopted a cooperative method across multiple areas such as art, education, therapy, and disability art, according to the website My Camden. Between 1981 and 1992, the Diorama Arts Centre (DAC) underwent significant changes and challenges. Following a request from the Crown Estate Commissioners (CEC), the Diorama Arts Centre was incorporated as a charity and a company on September 15, 1981. In 1982, a formal rental agreement was established, replacing the previously low peppercorn rent of approximately £25 per year. In 1983, the group encountered the risk of being evicted as Greycoats Estates, representing the CEC, intended to redevelop the Diorama into office premises. However, the Diorama Arts Centre fought against this attempted eviction and emerged victorious in 1984 after a public inquiry conducted by the Department of the Environment. The victory was aided by the 'Re-use of Industrial Buildings Service' provided by URBED (Urbanism, Environment, and Design Ltd.). By February 1984, the Diorama Arts Trust was formed to propose a scheme that led to a £4 million fundraising effort, extending beyond 1984. CAST (Cartoon Archetypical Slogan Theatre), led by Roland Muldoon, also agreed to support the cause, further strengthening the movement.

The concept of desire and its relationship to will is a fascinating one. Desire can be seen as the root from which will grows, and over time, will can become independent and even surpass its original source. This is particularly evident in habitual actions, where individuals often continue to perform certain actions out of habit, even when the original motivation has faded. This phenomenon is not limited to virtuous actions but can also apply to neutral or even harmful behaviors that have become ingrained over time. The distinction between will and desire is an important psychological fact. Will, like all aspects of our nature, is susceptible to habituation. We may find ourselves willing something not because we desire it, but simply because we have become accustomed to doing so. This is the power of habit, which can influence our actions even when they contradict our conscious preferences. In the case of virtue, a weak will can be strengthened by cultivating a desire for it. By associating virtuous actions with pleasure and vice versa, we can evoke a will to be virtuous that, once established, operates independently of the original motivations of pleasure or pain. Will is born from desire but eventually comes under the influence of habit. Although the result of habit might not always be morally positive, the consistency it brings to our emotions and actions is essential for maintaining a dependable will to act rightly. The principle of utility, which posits that happiness or pleasure is the ultimate good, is closely tied to this discussion. If we accept that will is driven by desire and habit, and that these in turn are influenced by pleasure and pain, then the principle of utility gains support. However, the validity of this principle is left for the reader to consider. The relationship between justice and utility presents another intricate matter. The strong sentiment associated with justice often leads people to view it as an absolute quality, distinct from the concept of expediency. Yet, the feeling of justice, like other instincts, may require guidance from a higher reason to ensure its appropriate application. The origin of the feeling of justice does not necessarily legitimize all its promptings. Even if justice is an instinct, it may still need to be controlled and enlightened by reason. The subjective feeling of justice may be different from that of simple expediency, but this does not mean that justice cannot be seen as a part of general utility. To understand the nature of justice, it is essential to examine whether the feeling of justice and injustice is unique or derived from other feelings. If the sensation of justice is determined to result from other emotions, it might be feasible to account for its strength and nature by means of the overarching principles governing our emotional makeup. When looking for shared features of just and unjust actions, it is essential to examine different cases. One common perception is that it is unjust to deprive someone of their personal liberty, property, or anything else that belongs to them by law. This perception, among others, will be explored further to determine the underlying qualities that define justice and injustice.

Sentimentalism, as a literary mode, has been a significant and recurring aspect of world literature, emphasizing emotions and feelings as the foundation of a person's actions and reactions, rather than reason. This literary movement encompasses various forms, including sentimental poetry, novels, and the German Empfindsamkeit music movement. European literary sentimentalism emerged during the Age of Enlightenment, partly as a response to sentimentalism in philosophy. In the 18th century, England witnessed the rise of the sentimental novel as a major literary genre. This development took place between 1730 and 1780, during the height of the Enlightenment, and subsequently spread to other European literatures. The philosophical underpinnings of sentimentalism primarily originated from Anthony Ashley Cooper, the 3rd Earl of Shaftesbury, who was a student of John Locke. Sentimentalism in both philosophy and literature can sometimes be challenging to differentiate, as they often influence and mirror each other. As literary works developed, they aimed to reflect these concepts by integrating them into stories and the portrayal of characters. Consequently, it is common to observe the coexistence of both philosophical and literary movements. Philosophically, sentimentalism was often juxtaposed with rationalism. While 18th-century rationalism focused on the development of the analytic mind as the basis for acquiring truth, sentimentalism emphasized the intrinsic human capacity for empathy, emotion, and moral sensibility. This literary mode sought to explore the depths of human emotions and the complexities of interpersonal relationships, providing a counterbalance to the rationalist approach of the time.

The French cavalry was renowned for its excellence, occupying an impressive fifteen square miles of land. Each cavalry company boasted one hundred and twenty horses, predominantly of the half-bred Percheron breed, with blacks and greys being the most common colors. A competitive spirit thrived among the companies, each striving to maintain the best-conditioned teams. These teams were frequently portrayed in artworks, illustrating the men performing different activities like cutting and felling trees. John Nash, a prominent British painter, emphasized the importance of an artist's visual acuity and manual dexterity. He believed that an artist's primary task is to train their eye to observe, probe, and then synchronize their hand movements with their visual perception. Nash's most renowned war painting, "Over the Top," is an oil on canvas of dimensions 79.4 x 107.3 cm and is presently exhibited at the Imperial War Museum in London. This artwork depicts the 30th December 1917 Welsh Ridge counter-attack, in which the 1st Battalion Artists Rifles (28th London Regiment) moved forward from their trenches toward Marcoing, near Cambrai. Tragically, of the eighty men involved, sixty-eight were either killed or wounded within the first few minutes of the assault. Nash himself was part of the twelve survivors who endured the intense machine gun fire portrayed in the artwork. He completed this powerful piece three months after the event. "Over the Top" offers a striking and intense depiction of soldiers moving into combat, clearly understanding the strong possibility of not surviving the encounter. Nash's depiction conveys the raw emotion and harsh reality of war, as he recounts the experience of soldiers falling to the ground, some with screams and others in silence, as their comrades continue to push forward.

Examen philosophicum, derived from Latin meaning "philosophic exam" and often abbreviated as Ex.phil., is one of two key academic examinations in the majority of undergraduate programs at Norwegian universities. It is complemented by the Examen facultatum, which focuses on teaching students the art of academic writing. In contrast, Examen philosophicum is intended to develop students' comprehension of philosophy and their capacity for structured thinking. The roots of Examen philosophicum date back to its establishment at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark-Norway in 1675. However, it was ceased in Denmark in 1971, and its existence in Norway has since diminished. The mandatory status of Examen philosophicum as a course is legally established through royal decrees particular to each university. For instance, the Regulations of 20 December 2005 No. 1798 on Studies and Exams at the University of Oslo serve as a legal basis for its implementation. Both Examen philosophicum and Examen facultatum are integral components of most bachelor's degree programs in Norway. Exceptions to this rule are mainly observed in professional programs at university colleges and a limited number of natural science programs at universities, which might be exempt from one or both examinations. The content of the Examen philosophicum may differ between universities and academic fields, often adapted to correspond with the scholarly emphasis of each department and the specific area of study within the undergraduate program. For example, students specializing in foreign languages will participate in a curriculum that is customarily adjusted to match their particular field of study. Generally, the Examen philosophicum encompasses the study of philosophy, ethics, and rhetoric. The University of Oslo maintained the tradition of Examen philosophicum, implementing it in 1812, which was two years following the university's founding. This academic examination continues to play a significant role in the Norwegian higher education system, fostering critical thinking and philosophical understanding among its students.

As they journeyed through the lush countryside of Hertfordshire and the verdant expanses of the Warwickshire coach roads, the man of the cloth noticed a subtle change in his companion, George Stobart. Despite the picturesque vistas and the warm embrace of the sun, Stobart seemed preoccupied, his gaze distant, his thoughts elsewhere. The seasoned traveler, known for his punctuality and politeness, was also renowned for his wide sympathies. He had quickly assessed Stobart's character and found it to be of true mettle. Yet, he could not help but express his concern about the young man's apparent distraction. "I hope you do not begin to tire of your work, Stobart," he said, his voice filled with genuine concern. "I have seen many young men start with fervor, only to lose their way when faith wavers. But I do not believe you are one of them. However, I sense that something troubles you." "I am troubled, sir," Stobart admitted, his voice heavy with worry. "I am troubled by a soul I am trying to win for Christ, but with little success." The seasoned man, with a keen insight, guessed the source of Stobart's concern. "It is about your cousin's widow, Lady Kilrush, is it not?" he asked, his gaze piercing. "You have told me of her generous nature and her unconventional beliefs. I understand your desire to bring her into the fold, out of gratitude for her support of your work among the poor." Stobart was taken aback by the man's intuition. "Indeed, sir, you have guessed correctly. I have tried to reason with her, but her commanding temper and her dismissive manner make it difficult. It seems that the forces of darkness have the upper hand, and it is easier to deny than to prove. When I am with her, I find myself forgetting the spiritual danger she is in, even as she saves others from physical suffering." The wise man chided Stobart gently. "You have focused too much on the woman and not enough on her soul. Her beauty has clouded your judgment. As your mentor and friend, I warn you against cherishing the company of a beautiful heathen unless your sole intent is her salvation." Stobart was quick to defend himself. "I assure you, sir, I have never entertained an unworthy thought about Lady Kilrush. She has always treated me with sisterly affection. Her beauty does not alter my concern for her soul. I would give half my life to save her from the dangers of worldly pleasures and the company of the unscrupulous." "If you can keep your conscience clear and win this woman from the clutches of Satan, you will have done well," the wise man advised. "But do not compromise the truth. If you fail to guide her towards righteousness, you must part ways with her forever." The conversation took a personal turn as the wise man shared his own experiences. "You know, Stobart, I too have known the pain of unrequited love. The woman I loved before Mrs. Wesley was a domestic servant, yet her intellect and character were worthy of the highest esteem. Circumstances prevented our union, and I made another choice." His voice trailed off with a sigh, revealing the depth of his unspoken sorrow. Stobart spent a month on the road with his mentor, preaching in Bristol and to the miners of Kingswood. They traveled from south to north, accompanied by one of Wesley's earliest and most gifted lay preachers. This humble man, despite his lowly birth, was a powerful orator, capable of stirring the hearts of those who had never heard the Word of God. The journey was filled with hardships and inconveniences, but the travelers bore them with good humor, inspired by Wesley's cheerful spirit and Christian contentment. By the time they reached London in May, Stobart had been away for over a month. He had received weekly letters from his wife, detailing her household concerns and their child's growth. He, in turn, wrote to her about his adventures, knowing she took great interest in the fine houses he visited and the social customs he observed. Their marriage, though devoid of the initial fervor of romantic love, was one of tranquil affection and mutual respect. Stobart believed he had chosen well in marrying the printer's daughter, as she allowed him the freedom to pursue his spiritual journey.
