I offer my hand only in friendship, and not for a fleeting moment, but for life. I appreciate your current gratitude, but do not let it cloud your judgment. I am still Norman the Devil, and you have seen my mark on the brows of your fallen enemies. I would gladly have your friendship, but I want it for the man I am, Norman of Torn, with all my faults and any virtues you may believe I possess." "You are correct, sir," the Earl agreed. "We are grateful for the service you have done for the House of Montfort, and you may always rely on our favor for as long as we live. We admire your bravery and honesty, but as long as you remain the Outlaw of Torn, you cannot dine at the table of De Montfort as a friend would." "Your words are those of a wise and cautious man," Norman of Torn replied calmly. "I shall leave, but remember that from this day forward, I have no quarrel with the House of Simon de Montfort, and should you ever need my assistance, my forces, numbering a thousand strong, are at your disposal. As he turned to depart, Bertrade de Montfort approached him, offering her hand in friendship. "You must accept my hand in friendship, for as long as I live, I will always be grateful to Norman of Torn for rescuing me from such a terrible fate." He took her fingers in his armored hand, knelt on one knee, and raised them to his lips. "To no other woman, man, king, God, or demon have I ever bowed the knee. If you ever need me, Lady Bertrade, remember that my services are yours to command." With that, he mounted his horse and rode silently from the courtyard of Leicester Castle, accompanied by his five hundred men. Without glancing back, Norman of Torn and his men disappeared around a curve in the road. A strange man," Simon de Montfort mused, "he is both good and bad, yet from today, I will always believe there is more good than bad in him. I wish he were different, for his strength would be a powerful weapon against the enemies of England if he could be persuaded to join our cause." "Who knows?" Henry de Montfort added. "Perhaps an offer of friendship might have led him to a better life. There was a hint of longing in his words. I wish, Father, that we had taken his hand.

Connivance refers to the act of conspiring or secretly agreeing with another party, particularly when there is an awareness of and consent to a wrongdoing or a distortion of the truth. It involves making something appear as something else, often for deceptive purposes. In a legal context, a determination of connivance may be issued when an individual has either actively or passively contributed to the act they are lodging a complaint regarding. In certain jurisdictions and for specific behaviors, a legal finding of connivance can have significant consequences. It may prevent the accuser from succeeding in their case. For instance, if a person induces their spouse to commit adultery, they might be barred from divorcing their spouse on the grounds of that adultery. This principle is illustrated in the case of Sargent v. The case of Sargent was heard in the Court of Chancery of New Jersey in 1920. The court ruled that a man who had not taken active steps to prevent his wife's adultery was not entitled to divorce her because he was a participant and consenter to her adultery. Connivance is closely related to the concept of collusive lawsuits, where parties to a legal dispute secretly agree to deceive the court or manipulate the legal proceedings for their own benefit. It is also associated with hypocrisy, as it involves the deliberate concealment of one's true intentions or beliefs. In conclusion, connivance represents a multifaceted legal principle that may lead to substantial impacts in different legal situations. It is essential to understand the nuances of connivance and its potential consequences to navigate the legal system effectively.

Bank Transfer Day was initiated in response to the introduction of excessive fees by major banks, most notably Bank of America's $5 monthly fee for debit card users and Wells Fargo's $3 charge for the same. The movement's Facebook page emphasizes the significance of the event, stating, "Together we can ensure that these banking institutions will always remember the 5th of November!! If the 99% withdraws their funds from the major banking institutions and transfers them to non-profit credit unions by this date, we will convey a strong message to the 1% that informed consumers will not back organizations engaging in unethical business practices. In 2009, finance writer and radio host Dave Ramsey expressed his preference for local community banks and credit unions, citing their excellent customer service and lack of involvement in the sub-prime mortgage crisis. Ramsey stated, "I haven’t done business with big banks for years, primarily because of the awful customer service you get at most of them. I like local, community banks, and I believe whole-heartedly in credit unions." Similarly, in 2009, financial expert Suze Orman criticized large banks for prioritizing shareholder profits over ethical business practices. She contrasted this with credit unions, which are accountable to their members and are generally considered "ethical and honest." Orman was quoted saying, "Large banks are often doing anything to increase earnings and profits for shareholders, while credit unions are generally more ethical and honest." In August 2011, consumer expert Clark Howard also urged his readers to be wary of "giant, monster megabanks" and to think about smaller banks or credit unions for better interest rates and customer service. Howard's advice aligns with the principles of Bank Transfer Day, which encourages consumers to shift their funds from major banks to non-profit credit unions as a means of protesting unethical business practices. The movement gained significant traction, with many consumers choosing to move their money from large banks to credit unions and smaller banks. This change functioned as a demonstration against high fees while also emphasizing the value of backing local financial institutions that focus on customer care and responsible business conduct.

The Dilbert Principle is a satirical management concept developed by Scott Adams, the creator of the comic strip Dilbert. It posits that companies often promote employees who lack competence to management positions in order to minimize their potential to negatively impact productivity. This idea is a lighthearted commentary on the Peter Principle, which claims that individuals are advanced in their careers due to their achievements until they attain a position where their abilities are no longer suitable. The Dilbert Principle was first introduced by Adams in a 1995 article for the Wall Street Journal and was further explored in his 1996 book, also titled "The Dilbert Principle." In the comic strip dated February 5, 1995, the character Dogbert humorously states that "leadership is nature's way of removing morons from the productive flow." Adams explained his rationale behind the principle, suggesting that in many cases, the least competent individuals are promoted to management roles because they are not desired for actual work. Instead, they are assigned tasks such as ordering supplies and overseeing others, while the more skilled employees, such as heart surgeons and computer programmers, are kept away from management roles. The Dilbert Principle serves as a critique of traditional corporate promotion practices, highlighting the potential flaws in promoting individuals based on past performance without considering their suitability for leadership roles. It encourages a reevaluation of how companies identify and develop talent for management positions, emphasizing the importance of competence and leadership skills over mere technical expertise.

Knowledge translation (KT) involves a complex process designed to connect research outcomes with their real-world use across different areas such as healthcare, farming, and schooling. The concept has evolved over time, with its roots traceable to early initiatives like the agricultural extension services established by the Smith-Lever Act of 1914 in the United States. The Smith-Lever Act established a partnership between U.S. land-grant universities and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to promote the spread of agricultural knowledge. Agricultural extension agents stationed at these universities were instrumental in disseminating information to farmers and ranchers regarding subjects like seed development, land management, and animal husbandry. In the health sector, the importance of KT has been recognized for decades. The National Center for the Dissemination of Disability Research (NCDDR) noted in their 2005 Technical Brief #10 that KT represents a relatively new term for an old issue: the insufficient application of evidence-based research within care systems. This underutilization often manifests as a gap between what is known through research and what is actually practiced in real-world settings. The influence of terminology on public perception and the uptake of information is also an important aspect of KT. For instance, the shift from using the term "swine flu" to "H1N1" has been observed to impact public understanding and response. Similarly, a study by Budhwani and Sun analyzed Twitter data to examine the rise in the use of the term "Chinese virus" to refer to the novel coronavirus. Their findings suggest that the increase in such references, along with the content of the tweets, may indicate that online platforms like Twitter could be perpetuating COVID-19 stigma and influencing knowledge translation. In summary, knowledge translation is a critical process that seeks to ensure that research findings are effectively communicated and applied in practice. It involves not only the dissemination of information but also the consideration of how language and public discourse can shape the way people understand and respond to new knowledge.

In Burmese schools, traditional attire is the norm for students. This comprises a blouse, which can be either the yinzi featuring a front opening or the yin hpon with a side opening, worn along with a green sarong referred to as a htamein and Burmese sandals. Public school teachers are also required to wear the same traditional attire as the students. In Namibia, school uniforms are prevalent in both private and state schools. In Nauru, schools mandate the wearing of uniforms by students. In Nepal, it is mandatory for students in both public and private schools to wear uniforms. Boys typically wear a shirt with long or short sleeves and long trousers in colors designated by their school. Girls' uniform frequently includes a blouse paired with a skirt in matching hues. Many Nepali schools mandate that students wear shoes, ties, and ID cards. There are strict policies regarding hairstyles, with long hair typically being tied in braids. The school uniform is regarded as an essential part of school life and is given significant importance. In the Netherlands, school uniforms are quite rare within the Dutch education system. Their use is generally limited to international and private schools. However, on the Caribbean islands of Bonaire, Saba, and Sint Eustatius, students at the only high schools on each island—Scholengemeenschap Bonaire, Saba Comprehensive School, and Gwendoline van Putten School—are required to wear uniforms. This article will be expanded to include information about school uniforms in New Zealand and other countries in the future.

Employee engagement and commitment are crucial for a company's success. To achieve this, organizations are increasingly turning to external partners, joint ventures, and merged or acquired companies for innovation, capabilities, and growth. The human resources (HR) function is essential in cultivating a culture that enables these external collaborations. Randy MacDonald, former Chief Human Resources Officer (CHRO) for IBM, summarized the findings of a recent study of HR leaders. According to the study, the three key workforce gaps that CHROs see as the biggest opportunities for HR are: 1. Cultivating creative leaders who can effectively navigate complex, global environments. 2. Mobilizing for greater speed and flexibility, which enhances the ability to adjust underlying costs and allocate talent more efficiently. 3. Leveraging collective intelligence by enhancing collaboration across more globally dispersed teams. Becoming a CHRO is a prestigious position within the HR field. Individuals who attain this role often have diverse work experiences, both within the HR function and in other areas. A 2011 survey of top HR leaders revealed that approximately two-thirds of CHROs had worked outside the HR function at some point in their careers. Additionally, there is significant movement between companies, with only 36% of US CHROs being promoted from within their own organization. In terms of HR experience, another survey highlighted that many CHROs have accumulated substantial experience in the field. This experience is often gained through various roles and industries, which helps them develop a broad perspective and a deep understanding of HR practices. This diverse background is essential for a CHRO to excel in their role and contribute to the overall success of the organization.

In Nigeria, business schools operate as colleges within traditional universities, providing a range of Master of Business Administration (MBA) programs. Additionally, several independent business schools in Nigeria collaborate with foreign institutions to offer MBA degrees. In South Africa, the Council on Higher Education (CHE) conducted a comprehensive re-accreditation of MBA programs in 2004. This process aimed to ensure the quality and standard of MBA education in the country. In Ghana, business schools at traditional universities provide a range of MBA programs. Moreover, foreign accredited institutions provide MBA degrees through distance learning, allowing more flexibility for students. In Kenya, MBA programs are available in numerous public and private universities. Students can specialize in areas such as accounting, finance, entrepreneurship, insurance, and human resources. The program typically spans four semesters, with each semester lasting approximately four months. In Asia, International MBA programs are gaining recognition and brand value. Although foreign MBAs are still popular in countries like the Philippines, many students are now enrolling in "Global MBA" programs taught in English. English-only MBA programs are available in several countries such as Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, and Thailand. To attract international students and foster a diverse learning environment, many Asian MBA programs provide scholarships and discounted tuition fees. Rankings for Asia Pacific business schools have been published by Asia Inc., a regional business magazine, to help prospective students make informed decisions about their education.

The implementation of the selective service draft stands as a monumental achievement, overshadowing all previous efforts to challenge the pacifistic inclinations of our populace. It is uncertain whether our people have experienced a profound psychological transformation, but it is evident that they have never before willingly submitted to conscription. For over a century, militias and volunteers formed the backbone of our land forces. During the Civil War, attempts at drafting led to riots, and throughout our history, enlistment bounties were a standard practice. Some might recognize General Upton's significant contribution, "Military Policy of the United States," which has only recently been brought to light. It, along with a subsequent publication, "The Military Unpreparedness of the United States," published around 1916, vividly highlights the inherent flaws of volunteering and offering bounties. However, it was only under the immense pressure of the great war that these long-standing theories were finally abandoned. We were fortunate to have a capable leader as Provost Marshal General in Enoch H. Crowder, who has been recognized with an honorary LL.D. degree by my alma mater, Princeton University, among others. Regardless of whether he was the originator of the draft system or if it was suggested by others, he was adept at identifying and implementing effective strategies. The challenge at hand was to register several million men aged 21 to 31, select those eligible for military service, and then draw a certain number by lot. The system used during the Civil War was grossly insufficient; army officers could not be spared for this task. So, how were the names to be collected, recorded, and drawn? General Crowder shared the origin of the fundamental plan with me on the day he received his degree from Princeton. He was in his office, deeply pondering a registry method that would not take an entire year to execute, when a Congressman visited and listened to his concerns. The conversation ended much like Alice's encounter with the Caterpillar in "Alice in Wonderland," who advised her on changing her height as it crawled away through the vegetation. As the unidentified Congressman was leaving, he casually remarked, "If they can elect a President in one day, they can register in one day." We are grateful that General Crowder had keen hearing and a sharp mind to grasp the implications of this statement. The existing election infrastructure, with its well-established hierarchy of states, counties, municipalities, and election districts, along with civil officers familiar with the people, presented a ready-made solution. All that was needed was to set it in motion. The spirited reaction from the forty-eight Governors, who maintained the secrecy until it was appropriate to notify local officials, resulted in the widely recognized outcome. Two additional factors were crucial: the willingness of men of draft age to report and the public's confidence in a fair drawing process. The latter was ensured by the use of master numbers for each district, while the former was a natural consequence of the system itself. Every man of draft age essentially became a volunteer, ready to report when called upon. The abolition of bounties and substitutes, which had plagued the old system, significantly contributed to this development. On this Fourth of July, we should be grateful for three significant achievements: the unity of Americanism, the leadership of our universities, and the establishment of a practical and widely accepted method for mobilizing the nation's manpower, setting a precedent for all time. A fourth achievement is the result of all these factors: a formidable army of young men, who will become future leaders in political life, deeply committed to the true freedom of our American system and determined to uphold it without tolerating any nonsense. Our awareness of this strength and faith in it is crucial, as it allows us to face the many troubling and dangerous issues currently at the forefront of our national life with less anxiety. Yet, within our success, there echo numerous signs of worry—indeed, many conflicting ones. Questions about the ratification of the treaty, the sustainability of peace, the reliability of the Germans in honoring their promises, and the potential need for the peace-loving nations to continue developing means of destruction in war, all demand our attention. Additionally, concerns about internal affairs, such as the stifling of individual enterprise and talent by regulations, the relevance of the United States Constitution, the role of the Senate, the threat of Bolshevik dictatorship, the impact of taxes and rate control on the transportation industry, and the future of the Monroe Doctrine, are all pressing issues that require resolution. These are not mere fantasies or partisan disputes; they are real and vital questions that need to be addressed, likely at a significant cost in both treasure and possibly blood. However, I have faith that they will ultimately be resolved correctly. It is essential to remember that our work is far from over and that our efforts during the war are only the beginning. We owe it to our country and our children to promote sanity, deliberation, and temperance in thought, speech, and action among all segments of the population.

Barter, originating from the word "baretor," refers to a trading system in which goods or services are directly traded for other goods or services without relying on a medium such as money. Economists distinguish barter from gift economies by highlighting that barter entails direct reciprocal exchanges at the moment of transaction, whereas gift economies involve exchanges that take place over a period of time. Barter transactions typically occur on a bilateral basis, but they can also be multilateral if facilitated through a trade exchange. In most developed countries, barter exists alongside monetary systems, but its usage is generally limited. It is often employed as an alternative to money during times of monetary crisis, such as when a currency becomes unstable due to hyperinflation or a deflationary spiral, or when money is simply unavailable for conducting commerce. It is essential to clarify that no ethnographic studies have demonstrated that any society, either present or past, has relied solely on barter without using any other medium of exchange or measurement. Anthropologists have also not found evidence to suggest that money originated from barter systems. Despite this, many economists, including Adam Smith (1723–1790), have inaccurately depicted pre-modern societies as examples of barter inefficiency to explain the emergence of money and the development of the economy. Adam Smith's economic theory sought to demonstrate that markets and economies predated the establishment of the state, and he contended that money was not an invention of the state but rather a natural progression from trade activities.

This study investigates the Epps effect within financial markets, with an emphasis on how time averaging and asynchrony influence correlation measurements. We challenge the traditional continuous-time models by employing a discrete-event simulation approach using multivariate Hawkes processes, which better capture the order-flow dynamics in markets. Our innovative contribution lies in extending the existing literature by examining the Epps effect through the lens of event-based processes, revealing nuances that continuous-time models overlook. We utilize Trade and Quote (TAQ) data from the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, carefully selecting a sample of ten equities to ensure a comprehensive analysis. Our approach incorporates several time averaging methods, including calendar time, intrinsic time, and volume time, to illustrate the reliability of our results under varying market circumstances. Our findings suggest that the Epps effect cannot be explained exclusively by lead-lag relationships or discrepancies in trade timing. Instead, we suggest that structural and hierarchical influences, arising from a combination of bottom-up and top-down market mechanisms, play a role in the observed variations in correlations. This insight suggests the need for a multi-scale approach to covariance estimation, as previously suggested by other researchers, to better understand the complex interplay of market dynamics across different time scales. The paper also critically evaluates the performance of different estimators, such as the MM and HY estimators, in the presence of market microstructure noise. We observe that the MM estimator exhibits a consistent Epps effect across different sampling intervals, whereas the HY estimator displays a weaker effect, especially when considering TAQ data. In summary, our study provides a new viewpoint on the Epps effect through the use of event-driven simulations and a multi-scale approach. This method not only deepens our comprehension of market behaviors but also establishes a more precise foundation for analyzing financial markets and managing risks. The findings underscore the importance of considering the discrete and asynchronous nature of financial markets when modeling and estimating correlations.

This section presents the main results of our research, which pertain to the asymptotic behavior of option prices and implied volatilities under various conditions. We begin by establishing moment conditions necessary for our analysis. For a given $\eta \in (0,\infty)$, we introduce two moment conditions. The first requires that the expected value of $e^{(1+\eta)X_t}$ remains bounded along a specified set of $(\kappa, t)$ values. When $t \le T$, it suffices to consider the expectation at $t = T$, as the process is a submartingale. The second moment condition involves the expectation of the absolute value of $(e^{X_t} - 1)/\kappa$ raised to the power of $(1+\eta)$, and simplifies for $\eta = 1$ to an inequality involving the expectation of $e^{2X_t}$. Our primary findings are encapsulated in two theorems. The first theorem examines right-tail asymptotics under the condition that the right tail probability $\F_t(\kappa)$ meets a particular hypothesis. We consider two scenarios: when $\kappa$ is bounded away from zero and $t$ is bounded away from infinity, and when both $\kappa$ and $t$ tend to zero. In the former case, we establish that the logarithm of the option price and the implied volatility exhibit specific asymptotic behaviors, which we express in terms of the tail probabilities. The latter scenario requires a weaker moment condition but leads to similar conclusions. The second theorem focuses on left-tail asymptotics, with conditions that are less restrictive than those for right-tail analysis. We again consider scenarios where $\kappa$ is bounded away from zero and $t$ is bounded away from infinity, and where both $\kappa$ and $t$ vanish. In both cases, we derive the asymptotic behavior of the option price and implied volatility. We then delve into the regime of typical deviations, where $t \to 0$ and $\kappa \to 0$ at a rate that ensures the tail probabilities have a strictly positive limit. We propose a hypothesis regarding the small time scaling and a related moment condition. Our results in this regime are presented in a theorem that links option prices and implied volatilities to tail probabilities, under the assumption that the random variable in the small time scaling converges to a Gaussian distribution. The innovative aspects of our research lie in the explicit expressions we provide for the asymptotic behavior of option prices and implied volatilities, which are derived under various conditions. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of the dynamics of financial markets, particularly in the context of option pricing and risk management. Our findings are supported by rigorous mathematical analysis and are applicable to a wide range of financial models.

This section delves into the optimal decision-making strategies for a planner within a financial framework, focusing on risk-return trade-offs. The Merton problem is presented, involving an individual's selection of an optimal investment approach to reconcile expected returns with associated risks. The paper extends this concept by considering a distribution of risk preferences across a population, leading to a parametric formulation that encapsulates the trade-off between risk and return. The payoff is decomposed into deterministic and stochastic components, illustrating how increasing the investment multiple, \( m \), escalates both returns and risks. The paper presents a utility function that reflects the power utility of agents who have different risk profiles, assuming a continuous and strictly positive distribution of these risk profiles. A key contribution of the research is the derivation of the certainty equivalent for an agent with a given risk type and decision \( m \), and the identification of the individually optimal decision, which is a function of the risk aversion level. The paper also introduces the concept of a planner's utility function, which may differ from that of the individual agents, and explores the implications of different forms of this utility function. The analysis then moves to characterizing optimal strategies for the planner, first considering a one-size-fits-all approach and then a more flexible scenario with multiple decision options. The paper presents a method to determine the optimal single decision for all agents, based on the distribution of risk types and the planner's utility function. It also examines the effect of the planner's aversion to inequality on the selected strategy, showing how varying degrees of aversion affect the trade-off between risk and return. The study presents a new method for modeling and determining optimal choices in an environment featuring diverse risk attitudes, providing guidance on how a planner can identify the most effective strategy for a varied group. The findings are presented in a clear and concise manner, facilitating understanding and application in real-world scenarios.

In this section, we examine the complexities of assessing longevity bonds and hybrid claims in the fields of insurance and finance. We conduct a comparative analysis of various valuation methods, emphasizing the compromises between market-consistent valuations and actuarial valuations. Our research contributes to the ongoing discourse on the appropriate valuation methodologies for insurance liabilities, especially in the presence of相依风险 (which translates to "dependent risks"). We begin by examining the pricing of longevity bonds, which are financial instruments designed to hedge against the risk of increased life expectancy. Using a comprehensive mathematical model, we show how the inclusion of these bonds can affect the variability and anticipated loss in an investment portfolio. Our findings indicate that although longevity bonds may lower risk, they also entail a cost that needs to be considered alongside the possible advantages. In the realm of hybrid claims, which combine both financial and actuarial risks, we propose a two-step valuation approach. This method allows for a more nuanced assessment of the value of these claims, taking into account the interplay between financial market conditions and actuarial uncertainties. We illustrate the application of this approach through an example involving equity-linked life insurance contracts, showcasing the differences in valuation outcomes under various assumptions about risk dependence. Our research emphasizes the importance of considering the specific characteristics of the risks being valued, as well as the broader economic context. We argue that neither market-consistent nor actuarial valuations can be deemed universally superior; rather, the choice of valuation method should be tailored to the particular needs and objectives of the insurer or investor. Innovative aspects of our research include the development of a two-step valuation framework that integrates financial and actuarial perspectives, and the exploration of the implications of risk dependence on valuation outcomes. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complexities involved in the valuation of insurance liabilities, particularly in the presence of相依风险 (dependent risks). We conclude with a numerical illustration that demonstrates the practical application of our two-step valuation approach. This example strengthens the conclusions drawn from our theoretical analysis, offering a tangible illustration of the significance of our research in practical settings. Through this work, we aim to enhance the dialogue on valuation practices within the insurance and finance sectors, offering a fresh perspective on the challenges and opportunities presented by evolving risk landscapes.

Digital games have been a subject of ongoing research for the past two decades, with findings indicating their potential as educational tools. The new generation seeks "multiple streams of information," which involves quick and frequent interactions that facilitate inductive reasoning. The popularity of games has led to the creation of a billion-dollar industry, emphasizing the importance of choice and enjoyment in engaging with these activities. Games go beyond being just recreational activities; they can also function as avenues for acquiring new skills, interacting with fellow players, and fully participating in an activity of interest. The element of choice is crucial for gamers, as it enhances their engagement and motivation. Kim (2008) supports integrating off-the-shelf games with meta-cognitive strategies to boost students' cognitive abilities. Educational entertainment extends beyond digital games, with radio and podcasts emerging as effective vehicles for imparting knowledge. The British radio soap opera "The Archers" has been educating its audience on agricultural matters for decades. In a similar vein, the Tanzanian radio soap opera "Twende na Wakati" ("Let's Go With the Times") was mainly crafted to advocate for family planning. Podcasts have also begun to exemplify the concept of edutainment, with some radio programs being adapted into this digital format. These series, integrating educational content, are enjoyed not just for leisure but also function as a tool for gaining knowledge and enhancing understanding. The integration of education with entertainment across various media platforms highlights the potential for engaging and effective learning experiences.

Sense-and-Respond Organizations is a concept that was introduced in a book published by Harvard Business School Press in 1993. The idea behind this organizational approach is to emphasize the importance of being agile and responsive to changes in the market and customer needs. This contrasts with the traditional "make and sell" approach, which focuses on producing products and then selling them to customers. The concept of "Managing by Wire," which was discussed in the Harvard Business Review in September-October 1992, is closely related to the sense-and-respond approach. The article, co-authored with R.L. Nolan, explores the use of information technology to facilitate more flexible and responsive management practices. In October, the American Management Association's Management Review published an article titled "From 'Make and Sell' to 'Sense and Respond.'" This piece further elaborates on the shift from a production-focused business model to one that is more attuned to sensing and responding to market dynamics and customer preferences. The sense-and-respond philosophy is about creating an organization that is capable of quickly adapting to changes in the external environment. This requires a culture that values innovation, collaboration, and continuous learning. By being more responsive to customer needs and market trends, organizations can better position themselves for success in a rapidly changing world.

Economic sanctions are a form of coercive diplomacy used by international organizations or individual countries to influence the behavior of a targeted state by imposing various restrictions. These can include military, economic, and trade embargoes, such as those on oil and petroleum products. The imposition of sanctions is often a response to a state's actions that are deemed unacceptable by the international community, such as human rights abuses or violations of international law. Sanctions can have significant impacts on the targeted country's economy and its citizens. While the primary goal of sanctions is to pressure the government to change its behavior, they can also lead to unintended consequences, such as exacerbating economic hardships for the general population. The effectiveness of sanctions in achieving their intended goals is a subject of ongoing debate among scholars and policymakers. Supporters of economic sanctions argue that they are a necessary tool for addressing international crises and promoting human rights. They contend that sanctions can serve as a deterrent to oppressive regimes and provide an alternative to military intervention. Advocates also point out that, in many cases, the citizens of a sanctioned country are already suffering under their government's policies, and that sanctions can help bring about positive change. However, opponents of sanctions claim that they might be unproductive and could potentially reinforce the determination of the targeted regime. Critics also raise concerns about the potential for sanctions to promote nationalistic sentiments and undermine the targeted state's culture. Furthermore, there is debate about the level of ethnocentrism involved in the design and implementation of sanctions, as well as the possibility that they may be driven by the self-interests of the countries imposing them. In some cases, sanctions may be imposed without a clear strategy for their removal or a well-defined end goal. This may result in an extended duration of economic difficulties for the people in the targeted nation, lacking a defined route to address the situation. It is essential for the international community to carefully consider the potential consequences of sanctions and to work towards a comprehensive approach that balances the need for accountability with the protection of human rights and the well-being of affected populations. Ultimately, the effectiveness of economic sanctions depends on a variety of factors, including the targeted state's level of dependence on the imposing countries, the unity of the international community in supporting the sanctions, and the targeted government's willingness to change its behavior in response to the pressure. As with any policy tool, the use of sanctions must be carefully weighed against their potential benefits and drawbacks, with the ultimate goal of promoting peace, stability, and respect for human rights around the world.

Social interdependence theory is a concept that explores the relationship between individuals' goals and their interactions within a group setting. The theory posits that the structure of participants' goals influences their interactions, which in turn, shapes the outcomes of the situation. There are three forms of interdependence: 1. Positive interdependence: Individuals work together to achieve common goals, fostering collaboration and mutual support. 2. Negative interdependence: Individuals perceive their goals as being in conflict with others, leading to oppositional or competitive interactions. 3. No interdependence: There is no perceived correlation between individuals' goal achievements, and they view their success as unrelated to others. Formal cooperative learning is a structured approach facilitated and monitored by an educator to achieve group goals in task work. It can be adapted to any course material or assignment and typically involves groups of 2-6 people. Discussions can range from a few minutes to an entire class period. Strategies for formal cooperative learning include: - The jigsaw technique: Students assume the role of a teacher for a specific topic and are responsible for teaching it to a classmate. This method encourages deep understanding of the material, as students must be able to teach it to others. - Group problem-solving and decision-making assignments: These tasks require collaboration and collective thinking to arrive at solutions or conclusions. - Laboratory or experiment assignments: Collaborative activities in a hands-on environment, where students combine their expertise and abilities to perform experiments or carry out investigations. - Peer review work: Students evaluate and provide feedback on each other's work, such as editing writing assignments. This process enhances critical thinking and fosters a deeper understanding of the subject matter. Developing experience and skill in formal cooperative learning often paves the way for informal and basic learning. By engaging in these activities, students not only learn the material but also develop essential skills such as communication, collaboration, and critical thinking.

Lean methodology has been recognized for its significant and measurable impact on improving academic and administrative operations within higher education institutions. The success of Lean can be seen at both the departmental/unit level and throughout the whole institution. However, it is important to note that implementing Lean requires a serious commitment and is most impactful when it involves long-term, strategic planning. While the application of Lean management in higher education is more prevalent in administrative processes such as admissions, registration, human resources, and procurement, it has also been increasingly applied to academic processes. These include course design and teaching, improving degree programs, student feedback, and the handling of assignments. Several innovative educational institutions have effectively adopted Lean methodologies, such as Cardiff University in Wales, Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, Michigan Technological University in the United States, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in the United States, University of Aberdeen in Scotland, University of Central Oklahoma in the United States, University of St. Andrews in Scotland, and Winona State University in the United States, along with other similar organizations. In the United Kingdom, a group of universities formed the LeanHEHub in 2012/2013. In 2016, the network underwent restructuring due to expansion and is now referred to as Lean HE - the Lean in Higher Education Network. Lean HE is divided into three continental regions: Lean HE Americas, Lean HE Europe, and Lean HE AsiaPacific. In addition, in Scotland, the Scottish Higher Education Improvement Network (SHEIN) functions as a collaborative network of higher education institutions dedicated to improvement.

Commissioner Anamarija Musa has been a significant figure in advancing the cause of access to public information in the 21st century. She has highlighted the challenges in implementing the law, particularly at the regional and local levels. One of the main issues is the difficulty in obtaining information from private entities that provide public services and from enterprises where the state holds a majority of the capital shares. According to Commissioner Musa, a concerning fact is that access to public information requests are often ignored. This has resulted in two-thirds of the complaints received by her office being due to this reason. The issue of access to public information is a crucial aspect of transparency and good governance. In Croatia, a web platform called "Imamo pravo znati" ("We have the right to know") has been launched to facilitate citizens' exercise of their right to access public information. Developed using the Alavetely software, the platform allows users to submit requests for public information to Croatian public authorities and track their responses. The platform also archives and makes publicly available the historic requests and any correspondence between the applicant and public authorities. Access to public information is a fundamental aspect of democratic societies. It promotes transparency, accountability, and informed decision-making. In Europe, various countries have enacted laws and regulations to ensure citizens' right to access public information. These laws are designed to protect the public's interest and promote openness in government operations. Freedom of information is a fundamental human right recognized by international law. It is essential for the protection of other human rights and for promoting transparency, accountability, and good governance. Freedom of information laws vary from country to country, with some offering more comprehensive protections than others. Another key factor in ensuring access to public information is the transparency of media ownership. In Europe, there have been efforts to promote transparency in media ownership to prevent concentration of media ownership and potential manipulation of information. In Croatia, the media landscape has undergone significant changes, and efforts have been made to increase transparency in media ownership. In conclusion, access to public information is a vital component of democratic societies. It promotes transparency, accountability, and informed decision-making. Commissioner Anamarija Musa's work and the "Imamo pravo znati" platform in Croatia are important steps in ensuring citizens' right to access public information. Efforts to promote freedom of information and transparency of media ownership in Europe and around the world are crucial for the protection of democratic values and human rights. References: 1. Access to Public Information in Europe 2. Freedom of Information Laws by Country 3. Transparency of Media Ownership in Europe 4. Media of Croatia 5.

Comparative Public Administration (CPA) is a sub-field of public administration that seeks to analyze and compare administrative systems and practices across different countries and cultures. Despite its potential for contributing to the development of more widely applicable policies, CPA has faced several challenges that have hindered its growth as a major field of study. One of the primary issues is the significant differences between Western and developing countries, which can make comparisons difficult. Additionally, the lack of a dedicated curriculum on comparative public administration in many public administration programs has limited the exposure and understanding of this sub-field among students and professionals. Another challenge is the absence of well-developed theoretical models that can be scientifically tested. This has resulted in a scattered and dated literature base, as noted by William Waugh, a professor at Georgia State University. He emphasizes the difficulty of comparative studies due to the need to provide sufficient information on the socio-political context of national administrative structures and processes to help readers understand the reasons behind observed differences and similarities. Despite these challenges, CPA continues to be a significant pursuit in the search for patterns and regularities in administrative actions and behaviors. The process of comparison allows for a deeper understanding of various administrative techniques and their applicability in different contexts. By fostering cross-cultural analysis, CPA can contribute to the development of more effective and adaptable public policies. In conclusion, Comparative Public Administration is a valuable yet underdeveloped sub-field of public administration. Its growth and recognition as a significant area of study would benefit from the development of a dedicated curriculum, the creation of robust theoretical models, and a concerted effort to update and expand the existing literature. By addressing these challenges, CPA can play a more prominent role in shaping public administration practices and policies worldwide.

A missing heir refers to a person connected to a deceased individual, who was the testator of a will, yet whose present residence, domicile, mailing address, or other contact details cannot be determined. This scenario often occurs in legal matters related to wills, property ownership, or quiet title proceedings. Missing heirs may consist of orphans or persons with disabilities who might need a guardian or custodian to handle their assets. In these situations, the executor, trustee, or administrator of the estate might hire a private investigator, probate research firm, or forensic genealogist to find the missing heir. When a missing heir is identified, a probate court or surrogate judge may mandate the service of legal documents such as a citation, notice of petition, summons, or subpoena to either the missing person or individuals who may have knowledge of their whereabouts. Some courts, like the Suffolk County Probate Court in Boston, actively seek out missing heirs. Probate research companies are specialized in finding missing and unknown heirs, assisting in the resolution of legal matters related to estates and inheritance. Their expertise is invaluable in ensuring that the rightful heirs are identified and their interests are protected in accordance with the law.

The case of Thorogood v Bryan involved a tragic incident where a passenger was killed after being dropped off in the middle of the road by an omnibus. The deceased was unable to move out of the way in time and was subsequently run over by another omnibus traveling at a high speed. The drivers of both vehicles were found guilty of negligence. However, the court ruled that the plaintiff could not recover damages, based on the principle that a passenger is considered to have identified with the vehicle he is traveling in. If the driver is negligent, his fault is imputed to the passenger. In a different case, Mills v Armstrong, a collision occurred between the steamships Bernina and Bushire, leading to the death of Armstrong, who was the first engineer on the Bushire. The accident was due to the carelessness of the individuals responsible for both vessels. The personal representatives of Armstrong brought an action against the owner of the Bernina to recover damages for his death. Initially, it was argued that the plaintiff could not recover based on the principle established in Thorogood v Bryan. However, the House of Lords reversed this principle, determining that the case of Thorogood v Bryan had been incorrectly decided. It is crucial to recognize that a mistaken judgment does not form a valid legal precedent. As stated by Bronson J in Butler v Van Wyck, an incorrect ruling may be final for the parties involved in the case, but it does not set a precedent for future cases. This highlights the importance of continuous review and reinterpretation of legal principles to ensure justice is served accurately and fairly.

Despite manufacturers' implementation of voluntary agreements, independent repair companies continue to encounter difficulties in obtaining spare parts and diagnostic equipment. A study by the Terrance Group revealed that approximately 59% of these services still struggle to obtain diagnostic tools and parts. However, the push for a "right to repair" has been gaining momentum in both the automotive and other industries, with increasing legislative proposals and court decisions. Initially, the movement was primarily driven by automotive consumer protection agencies and the automotive after-sales service industry. As consumer electronics like smartphones and computers became widely available, the discussion expanded to include a broader range of industrially produced devices. The movement has also been supported by climate change activists, who argue that allowing repairs would help reduce electronic waste. Despite these efforts, manufacturers have continued to implement measures that effectively restrict the rights of owners to repair their devices. Practices such as part pairing, where components of a device are serialized and cannot be replaced with non-matching parts, have become increasingly common. This has led to issues even with routine repairs, such as the replacement of a smartphone display, which can cause malfunctions due to the implemented locks. The right to repair movement seeks to address these challenges and promote greater accessibility to repair services for consumers, while also considering the environmental benefits of reducing electronic waste. As the debate continues, it remains to be seen how the legislative and judicial branches will respond to these concerns and whether independent repair companies will gain the necessary support to overcome the current obstacles.

The Chief Risk Officer (CRO) holds a crucial position across multiple industries such as finance, insurance, and more. Watson's analysis indicates that possessing outstanding analytical skills by itself is insufficient for achieving success as a CRO. Instead, the most effective CROs are those who can integrate their analytical prowess with strong commercial, strategic, leadership, and communication skills. These individuals are skilled in facilitating organizational transformation and achieving substantial influence. Typically, CROs possess post-graduate qualifications and have amassed over two decades of experience in fields such as accounting, economics, law, or actuarial science. Their role involves a delicate balance of risks against various factors like finance, investment, insurance, personnel, and inventory management to achieve an optimal level that satisfies all stakeholders. A study conducted by Morgan McKinley highlights that an effective Chief Risk Officer needs to be able to manage complexity and uncertainty while keeping a clear grasp of the overall context. James Lam, a prominent risk professional, is recognized for coining the term "Chief Risk Officer." He was the first to hold this position at GE Capital in 1993. The role gained prominence following the implementation of the Basel Accord, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, and the Turnbull Report. A CRO's primary responsibility is to ensure full compliance with all applicable regulations and to meticulously analyze all risk-related issues. They frequently work alongside other top-level officials, including the Chief Compliance Officer, to tackle subjects related to insurance, internal auditing, corporate investigations, fraud, and information security. This multifaceted role demands a deep understanding of an organization's operations and the ability to navigate the complex landscape of risk management.

The idea of competency includes a variety of values, attitudes, knowledge, abilities, skills, experiences, and behaviors that support successful performance across different tasks. The ARZESH Competency Model (2018) describes competency as an amalgamation of these components, which can be cultivated via training and evaluated for assessment purposes. Competencies may be divided into finer, more detailed elements to enhance comprehension and assessment of an individual's abilities. Javier Perez-Capdevila further refined the definition of competencies in 2017, describing them as a fusion of the various aptitudes and attitudes possessed by employees, both in general and specific contexts. The degree of belonging to the resulting group indicates the extent to which these competencies are possessed by an individual. In the realm of human resource management, competency serves as a broader description of the requirements for individuals within organizations and communities. Competency models can be applied universally to all employees or tailored to specific positions within an organization. It is important to differentiate between job competencies and job tasks. Job competencies encompass the entire set of knowledge, skills, abilities, and attributes that contribute to a person's success in their role. These competencies are not limited to the specific tasks assigned but include the context-specific qualities that are correlated with superior job performance. Competencies can be used as a standard against which to measure an individual's job performance, providing a comprehensive assessment of their capabilities and potential for growth within their role. By understanding and evaluating competencies, organizations can better identify areas for development and create opportunities for employees to enhance their skills and contribute more effectively to the organization's goals.

The Policy Governance model, developed by John Carver, emphasizes the importance of continuous training and support for its effective implementation. Some individuals may misconceive the model's distinction between 'ends' and 'means,' assuming a rigid division of responsibilities. According to this misconception, the board should solely concentrate on 'ends,' while management should focus on the 'means' to achieve those ends. However, a careful examination of the model reveals that this interpretation is not accurate. Carver asserts that the board is accountable for all aspects, including both ends and means. Therefore, the ends/means distinction does not exempt the board from any responsibilities. Instead, the board must exercise control over both, ensuring that the organization's activities align with its goals and values. Another frequent misunderstanding is the idea that boards adhering to Carver's model ought not to engage with the organization's operational specifics. This notion stems from Carver's warning against excessive interference in operational matters. However, Carver clarifies that boards are still accountable to their stakeholders for all operational aspects and must maintain control over them. To strike a balance between accountability and avoiding excessive intrusion, Carver recommends the use of 'nested sets' of expectations. These sets are articulated in increasingly specific policy language, allowing the board to define its expectations with greater precision. The process continues until the board reaches a point where it can accept any reasonable interpretation of the policy, ensuring that the organization's activities remain within the desired parameters. In summary, the Policy Governance model promotes a clear understanding of the board's responsibilities and the effective management of an organization's operations. It encourages boards to maintain control over both ends and means while avoiding unnecessary interference in day-to-day activities. By adopting a nuanced approach to policy-making and monitoring, boards can ensure that their organizations fulfill their intended purposes and achieve their goals.

Roads are a critical component of transportation systems worldwide, with a significant percentage of both goods and people relying on them for movement. About 44% of all goods are carried by trucks on roads, whereas a remarkable 85% of individuals use cars, buses, or coaches for travel. In the past, the word "road" has also referred to roadsteads, which are water passages appropriate for sea travel. The construction of multi-lane roads can be costly, with per-mile costs varying significantly depending on the location and specific project. According to the New York State Thruway Authority, some sample costs for constructing multi-lane roads in the northeastern United States include: - Connecticut Turnpike: $3,449,000 per mile - New Jersey Turnpike: $2,200,000 per mile - Pennsylvania Turnpike (Delaware Extension): $1,970,000 per mile - Northern Indiana Toll Road: $1,790,000 per mile - Garden State Parkway: $1,720,000 per mile - Massachusetts Turnpike: $1,600,000 per mile - Thruway, New York to Pennsylvania Line: $1,547,000 per mile - Ohio Turnpike: $1,352,000 per mile - Pennsylvania Turnpike (early construction): $736,000 per mile These figures highlight the substantial financial investment required to build and maintain road infrastructure. In terms of road network size, the United States boasts the largest network globally, with 4,050,717 miles (6,518,997 km) of roads as of 2009. India comes in next, possessing the second-largest road network, which spans 4,689,842 kilometers (2,914,133 miles) as of 2013. China is ranked third, having 3,583,715 kilometers (2,226,817 miles) of road in 2007, whereas Brazil is in fourth place with 1,751,868 kilometers (1,088,560 miles) of road in 2002. For a more complete comparison, consult the List of countries by road network size. When focusing specifically on expressways, China's National Trunk Highway System (NTHS) spans an impressive 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles), showcasing the extensive reach of this critical transportation infrastructure.

The European Operations Management Association (EurOMA) is an international network comprising academics and practitioners who share a common interest in the ongoing development of Operations Management. With its roots in Europe, EurOMA has established a rapidly expanding network of international connections. This network facilitates the exchange of ideas, knowledge, and experience among its members, bridging the gap between research and practice. EurOMA collaborates with its counterparts in the United States and Japan, namely the Production and Operations Management Society (POMS) and the Japanese Operations Management and Strategy Association (JOMSA). Together, these organizations strive to extend the reach of Operations Management globally by fostering closer connections among professionals in the field. The organization focuses heavily on the creation and use of knowledge within Operations Management. It believes that excellence in manufacturing and service operations can be achieved through the advancement of new knowledge. EurOMA serves as a focal point for identifying, disseminating, and exploring the latest thinking and research in the field. This function contributes to defining future directions in Operations Management research. One of the key platforms for showcasing new ideas and developments in the field is the International Annual EurOMA Conference. This significant gathering offers a platform for experts to share their findings and interact with colleagues through dialogue. In addition to its research and networking activities, EurOMA is committed to supporting education in Operations Management. The association promotes a wide range of academic initiatives aimed at enhancing the teaching and learning of Operations Management principles and practices. Through these efforts, EurOMA contributes to the growth and development of the field, ensuring that it remains at the forefront of innovation and excellence.

The case of Harvey, a convicted individual, centered on the legal intricacies surrounding the Brady v. Maryland ruling, which pertains to the discovery of exculpatory evidence. Harvey claimed that he was not in a position to invoke this ruling, as he could not demonstrate that a state actor had infringed upon a federally protected right. This assertion was based on the procedural aspects of the case rather than the merits of the claim itself. In the aftermath of a January 2002 decision, Harvey sought DNA testing through Virginia's Fairfax Circuit Court, leveraging a 2001 law that expanded felons' access to biological evidence that had not been previously analyzed with contemporary DNA testing techniques. The court responded favorably to this request, and on March 1, 2002, directed the Division of Forensic Science to carry out the necessary tests. Upon completion of the DNA testing on May 15, 2002, the Division of Forensic Science submitted a certificate of analysis. This document indicated that Harvey could not be ruled out as a potential source of the sperm fractions identified on the victim. Consequently, on September 24, 2002, Harvey escalated his legal challenge by filing a petition for a writ of habeas corpus with the Virginia Supreme Court. This petition contested the validity of the certificate of analysis and the associated test outcomes. However, the court dismissed the petition on June 10, 2004, citing a lack of jurisdiction to entertain the matter. In March 2002, the federal appeal was deliberated by the full Fourth Circuit in an en banc session, which is a reconsideration by all judges of the court rather than a smaller panel. By this juncture, the original issue had become moot. Despite this, two judges, J. Michael Luttig and Judge Wilkinson, chose to contribute their perspectives. Luttig highlighted the importance of the "right of access to" within the case context, even though the precise aspects of his argument are not included in the excerpt.

The concept of "pay-what-you-want" (PWYW) has gained significant traction in the music industry, allowing artists to offer their work at a price determined by the consumer. This creative method has been adopted by numerous artists and groups, each applying the model in their own distinct manner. One notable example is Jane Siberry, who confirmed in an interview with The Globe and Mail that her self-determined pricing policy has resulted in an average income per song that is slightly higher than the standard price. This demonstrates the potential for PWYW to be a viable revenue stream for artists. Jeff Rosenstock, who is the lead singer of the New York punk groups The Arrogant Sons of Bitches and Bomb the Music Industry!, started distributing his music via his digital-only record label, Quote Unquote Records, in 2005. The label's releases are available as free downloads, with an option for listeners to make a donation. The website proudly proclaims itself as "The First Ever Donation Based Record Label." Bandcamp, a web service launched in 2007, has also integrated the PWYW model into its platform. Musicians can sell their music directly to fans or simply upload it for streaming. Fans have the option to name their own price when purchasing music, and bands have the ability to set minimum prices for their work. Buyers can pay any amount over the minimum price, providing flexibility for both artists and consumers. In a groundbreaking move, the English band Radiohead released their seventh album, In Rainbows, in October 2007 using a PWYW system through their website. This was the initial instance where a prominent music group implemented the PWYW approach, increasing visibility and generating enthusiasm for the idea. In 2008, Wheatus transitioned to a PWYW system for all their future and past albums for which they held the rights. The comedy kids/hip hop duo Koo Koo Kanga Roo has also adopted the PWYW model for their music releases. The use of the pay-what-you-want model by these artists and bands demonstrates its capacity as a versatile and adjustable method for distributing music. It allows artists to connect with their audience in a more personal way while providing fans with the freedom to support their favorite musicians according to their means.

In the realm of legal interpretation, various methods have been developed to understand and apply laws accurately. One of the fundamental principles is "Noscitur a sociis," which means "a word is known by its associates." This principle suggests that the meaning of a term can be understood by considering the context in which it is used. Another important concept is "in pari materia," which refers to the interpretation of a legal provision in light of other laws dealing with the same subject matter. Legal interpretation may be classified as common, technical, legal, or trade definitions based on the context. European perceptions of legal interpretation have evolved over time. The French philosopher Montesquieu (1689–1755) advocated for courts to act as "the mouth of the law," emphasizing the importance of adhering to the text. However, it soon became apparent that some level of interpretation is inevitable. Drawing from the work of German scholar Friedrich Carl von Savigny (1779–1861), four main methods of legal interpretation have been identified: 1. Grammatical interpretation: This method focuses on the literal meaning of the statutory text, emphasizing the importance of the words used and their ordinary understanding. 2. Historical interpretation: This approach examines the legislative history to reveal the intent of the legislator, providing insight into the purpose behind the law. 3. Systematic interpretation: This approach takes into account the context of provisions, including their location within a specific chapter or section of the law, in order to determine their intended use. 4. Teleological interpretation: This approach takes into account the purpose of the statute (Latin: ratio legis), as derived from legislative history or other relevant observations. The question of whether there is a hierarchy between these interpretation methods remains controversial. In Germany, there is a preference for a "grammatical" or literal interpretation, as the statutory text is seen as having democratic legitimacy. Deviating from this text is considered risky, particularly in light of German history. The term "sensible" interpretation can be subjective and may lead to varying interpretations. In contrast, the modern common law perception holds that courts not only interpret but also make law. This perspective differs significantly from the German view, where courts are seen as having the role of further developing the law (Rechtsfortbildung) rather than creating it. Ultimately, the choice of interpretation method may depend on the specific legal system, the nature of the case, and the values and principles that underpin the legal culture. It is essential for legal professionals to be familiar with these methods and to apply them judiciously to ensure a fair and accurate application of the law.

In Pakistan, local governance is structured through a hierarchy of elected officials, including Nazims of Union Councils, Union Councillors, and Tehsil Nazims. These individuals are chosen by the local public through direct voting in council elections, which occur every four years. In the Philippines, mayors play a crucial role, acting as the chief executive of a municipality or city, while the vice mayor occupies the next highest rank. Elections for these positions take place every three years during the midterm and national elections, allowing mayors to serve up to three consecutive terms. As of September 2012, there were 1,635 mayors in the country. Poland's local government system is composed of municipalities, known as gminas. As of April 30, 2022, there are 2,477 gminas in total, which include 1,513 rural gminas and 968 urban gminas that encompass cities and towns. Among these, 666 towns are part of an urban-rural gmina, while 302 cities and towns operate as standalone urban gminas. This latter group consists of 107 cities governed by a "prezydent miasta" (city mayor), with 66 cities possessing powiat rights. Within this subset, 37 cities have a population exceeding 100,000, and 18 of these cities serve as seats for voivode or voivodeship sejmik, often referred to as voivodeship cities. All municipalities in Poland, whether urban or rural, operate under a mandatory mayor–council government system. The executive power within these municipalities is held by officials known by various titles, depending on the type of municipality: - A city mayor (prezydent miasta) - A town mayor (burmistrz) - A wójt, which is the equivalent office in a rural municipality (gmina wiejska) These officials are elected through a two-round voting system.

The physical demands of certain professions can be grueling, and this is particularly true for women who are increasingly taking on roles that require significant physical and mental exertion, such as teaching. College students often idolize physical strength, with athletes receiving more attention and praise than the most accomplished scholars or educators. This fleeting fame is short-lived, often leading to obscurity once the individual is no longer in the public eye. Educators must strive to instill a more accurate understanding of values, emphasizing the importance of intellectual and moral development over physical prowess. The appreciation for the value of things, especially money, tends to develop more slowly. Boys, in particular, often struggle with understanding how to manage their finances effectively. They are prone to the misconception that they can have both this and that, rather than making a choice between the two. To counteract this, students should be given opportunities to gain experience with financial management on a small scale, learning to value not just in monetary terms, but also in terms of the inconvenience of going without. While cautions against extreme thriftiness are seldom needed, certain boys might develop such habits through observation or due to their personal inclinations. If these tendencies are not addressed by the student's own sense of honor, they become a part of moral education. The establishment of school savings banks is a modern approach to teaching children the importance of money and the benefits of saving. This encourages the development of a saving habit while also reducing impulsive spending. If self-indulgence, coupled with stinginess towards others, becomes a habit in childhood and youth, it can lead to significant unhappiness in later life, with spouses and children often suffering as a result. With women now being the primary educators of children, they should be mindful of the importance of instilling appropriate ideals and habits regarding the accumulation and expenditure of money. No form of selfishness is more detestable than indulging oneself at the expense of those who have a rightful claim to a fair share of resources. By consistently highlighting the unattractiveness of such behavior, its prevalence can be reduced. As students gain experience and learn to navigate the pressures of society, they must also learn to discern which honors, objects, and enjoyments they can or must do without. The thoughtful student will quickly realize that one thing often enables or conditions another. However, for those who do not grasp this concept readily, the teacher must assist in reinforcing this understanding, as a person without a clear perspective on these matters lacks character. It is frequently advantageous for students to retain some flexibility in their interests and moral and religious convictions, since this constitutes a component of the development of intellectual and moral awareness. The objective aspects of character should not become fixed too soon, and much of the value of education lies in delaying this process. Regulative training should begin as soon as the subjective aspects of character start to emerge. During the early stages of a child's development, it is best not to argue with them, but this approach must be abandoned once the child begins to reason for themselves. At this point, their thoughts become more coherent and permanent, and it is crucial for the educator to engage with the child's thought processes, guiding them away from incorrect conclusions. The teacher must be patient and allow for open discussion, even if it leads to inconvenient debates. It is important to accept a student's genuine concerns and refrain from suppressing their voice. In cases where immediate agreement is unattainable, the teacher should defer judgment, acknowledging the student's lack of knowledge and encouraging them to seek further understanding through future studies. The assertion of certainty by young people is often rooted in their ignorance, as they are unaware of the multitude of opinions that have been debated throughout history. Education will gradually help them overcome their overconfidence. In a society that values personal and political freedom, unquestioning obedience to authority is not acceptable. The development of subjective character demands a rejection of such methods. In a nation valuing leadership and self-rule, education ought to emphasize both obedience and the cultivation of leadership skills. Argumentation should be encouraged when it serves to clarify a student's understanding of prudence or duty. While obedience without question may be expected in relation to basic school virtues such as punctuality and diligence, more complex moral issues should be explored through dialogue. The ultimate goal of training is to establish regulatory principles in the minds of older students, enabling them to become self-governing within their capacity. This gradual progression towards moral autonomy is the essence of Herbart's approach to moral education. What Kant considered an unsolvable problem can be seen as a natural developmental process. By promoting a progressive grasp of moral principles, students can come to exercise their freedom and develop into self-governing citizens.

A pauper's oath is a formal statement or promise made by someone in a condition of severe poverty, commonly called a "pauper." This individual might not have the money to pay court expenses, a situation also termed "indigence." In these situations, the person can choose to take a pauper's oath, enabling them to initiate a legal case without needing to cover the filing fees. This practice is particularly common among prisoners, who are frequently without access to funds or the means to obtain any. Historically, the pauper's oath played a significant role in the United States, especially during the Great Depression. It was often required as a prerequisite for individuals to receive welfare assistance. Under U.S. federal law, one example of a pauper's oath used to establish indigent status is as follows: "I do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I have not any property, real or personal, exceeding $20, except such as is by law exempt from being taken on civil process for debt; and that I have no property in any way conveyed or concealed, or in any way disposed of, for my future use or benefit." The phrase "So help me God" may be included at the end of the oath, but this is optional. The concept of a pauper's oath is closely related to other legal and social topics, such as bankruptcy and poverty. It also has parallels in the legal principle of "in forma pauperis," which allows individuals who cannot afford to pay court fees to pursue legal action without incurring financial costs. References: - For a comprehensive understanding of the historical context and implications of the pauper's oath, consider consulting primary sources from the era of the Great Depression, as well as scholarly articles that analyze the legal and social implications of this practice. - Legal textbooks and case law can provide further insight into the current application of the pauper's oath and the principle of in forma pauperis in the U.S. legal system.

The Socrates-Erasmus Programme is a European Union initiative designed to promote educational exchanges across European universities. It aims to foster intercultural understanding and cooperation among students, educators, and institutions by providing opportunities for study and teaching placements in participating countries. In addition to the Socrates-Erasmus Programme, other organizations and programs also contribute to the internationalization of education. The Soros Foundation, for instance, offers various opportunities for students from Central Asia and Eastern Europe. Established by philanthropist George Soros, the foundation supports education, civil society development, and critical thinking in these regions. The International Baccalaureate (IB) is another significant player in the realm of international education. It is a globally recognized educational program that provides a challenging and comprehensive curriculum for students aged 3 to 19. The IB encourages critical thinking, cultural awareness, and a dedication to continuous learning. The global campus online, spearheaded by American universities, represents another innovative approach to international education. This platform allows students from around the world to access class materials, lecture files, and other educational resources for free. By making these resources available online, the global campus online breaks down geographical barriers and enables students to engage with diverse perspectives and ideas. To ensure the quality and effectiveness of international education, organizations such as the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) and the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement (IEA) play a crucial role.
