In 1901, it was found that large amounts of radiation could lead to harm in humans. The French physicist Henri Becquerel conducted an experiment where he carried a sample of radium in his pocket. This resulted in a highly localized dose of radiation, causing a radiation burn. This incident led to further investigation into the biological properties of radiation, which eventually contributed to the development of medical treatments. Ernest Rutherford, working in Canada and England, made significant contributions to the understanding of radioactive decay. He formulated a simple equation, now known as first-order kinetics, to describe the process. This equation revealed that a given radioactive substance has a characteristic "half-life," which is the time taken for the radioactivity present in a source to decrease by half. Rutherford also introduced the terms alpha, beta, and gamma rays to categorize different types of radiation. He is well-known for transforming nitrogen into oxygen via a sequence of experiments. Most notably, he oversaw the students who performed the Geiger-Marsden experiment, commonly referred to as the gold foil experiment. This experiment refuted the "plum pudding model" of the atom, which was introduced by J.J. Thomson in 1904. The plum pudding model suggested that an atom consists of electrons surrounded by a cloud of positive charge to balance the electrons' negative charge. However, the gold foil experiment indicated that the positive charge is concentrated in a very small nucleus. This discovery led to the development of the Rutherford model of the atom, which was later refined by the Bohr model. In the Bohr model, the positively charged nucleus is encircled by electrons that carry a negative charge. In 1934, Irène Joliot-Curie, the daughter of Marie Curie, along with her spouse Frédéric Joliot-Curie, carried on the work within the field of radioactivity. They人工合成了放射性同位素 and conducted further research that expanded the understanding of nuclear reactions and the properties of radioactive elements.

Johann Bürgi, a pioneering figure in the field of mathematics, sought to revolutionize the way trigonometric functions were understood and applied. In his own words, Bürgi expressed his belief that the traditional methods used by his ancestors were cumbersome and laborious, and he aimed to develop a more efficient and accurate approach. Bürgi's innovative ideas were centered around the concept of dividing a right angle into multiple parts, allowing for the calculation of sines without the need for complex inscriptions of polygons. This breakthrough had the potential to simplify the process of finding trigonometric values and make it more accessible to a wider audience. His seminal tables, which he developed, were included in his book "Fundamentum Astronomiæ" and published approximately between 1586 and 1587. These tables represented a significant advancement in the field of trigonometry and laid the foundation for future developments in mathematics. It is important to note that Bürgi's work was not developed in isolation. His ideas were influenced by the works of other prominent mathematicians and astronomers, such as Ptolemy in his "Almagest" and the mysterious Plimpton 322, an ancient Babylonian clay tablet that contains a trigonometric table. In conclusion, Johann Bürgi's contributions to the field of trigonometry were groundbreaking and have had a lasting impact on the way we understand and apply mathematical concepts today. His innovative approach to dividing a right angle and his development of trigonometric tables have made a significant and lasting contribution to the field of mathematics.

In this study, we performed a detailed examination of the GLIMPSE catalog, recognizing multiple OH/IR stars along with their respective locations. Notably, OH0.3$-$0.2 was identified because of its unique redness and luminosity in the TIR, consistent with its SIMBAD database entry as OH0.335$-$0.180. Discrepancies were observed in the reported NIR spectrum of OH$0.335-0.180$, which we attribute to a different object, 2MASS J17470734$-$2844282. Our approach included cross-checking the SIMBAD database against other catalogs, including the OH maser source catalog by \citet{1997A&AS..122...79S}, to locate and verify the positions of OH/IR stars. For instance, OH1.5$-$0.0 was identified based on its position and characteristics, matching SSTGLMC G001.4837$-$00.0612, which exhibited a notably red color in the NIR. We also recognized OH11.5+0.1, OH15.7+0.8, and OH17.7$-$2.0 by combining their locations in the SIMBAD database, their luminosity in the 2MASS and IRAC images, and their unique red coloration. In some cases, such as OH18.3+0.4, the absence of the object in the 2MASS images, coupled with its prominence in the IRAC images, indicated a very red characteristic typical of OH/IR stars. For OH359.4$-$1.3, a bright TIR source was identified in the IRAC band 4 image, aligning with the OH maser source listed in the catalog by \citet{1997A&AS..122...79S}. The UKIDSS K-band image further supported this identification by revealing two barely resolved sources, prompting us to regard the dimmer of the two as the TIR/OH maser source. In the following archival data analysis, we investigated the long-term brightness variation of non-variable OH/IR stars utilizing data from the 2MASS PSC, the UKIRT Infrared Deep Sky Survey (UKIDSS), and the Okayama Astrophysical Observatory Wide Field Camera. Our results enhance the comprehension of the properties and locations of OH/IR stars, offering a useful asset for additional astronomical studies.

In this study, we introduce novel metrics—$T_c$, $W$, and $S$—to differentiate between populations and species based on the total number of individuals. These metrics allow us to detect spontaneous symmetry breaking in biological systems. Specifically, $S$ measures the degree of orderliness based on dominance. Our approach not only identifies the critical point $T_c$ and the Weiss field $W$ but also distinguishes between various ordering states, such as random distribution, dominance of a particular species or population, and their potential phase transitions, including adaptations where $T_s \approx W$. This situation parallels the biological use of Bose-Einstein condensation in population dynamics, a notion that has been examined before but with a distinct variation illustrated in Figure 3. Our model reveals that the phase separation is contingent upon the levels of biological hierarchies, such as populations and species. It enables us to assess the adaptive structures that emerge during evolution at different stages. For instance, in a population-dominant phase, a single population could monopolize a community, whereas in a species-dominant phase, the collective of a particular species, rather than a single population, could prevail. The progression of phases corresponds to the emergence of new dominance patterns, with the chaotic phase's outcomes being inherently unpredictable. The model also indicates that some highly adapted species exhibit greater stability than others. Intriguingly, the zero points of the Riemann zeta function correspond to both adaptive species and prime numbers. The entropy $\ln k$, introduced in this manuscript, can be approximated by $\pi (k)/k \approx 1/\ln k$, where $\pi(k)$ denotes the prime counting function. The interplay between the diminishing prime number density and the increasing entropy suggests that the trend is disrupted only by the presence of higher-order hierarchies. For these organisms, higher-order hierarchies could function as facilitators for adaptive ordered structures. The originality of our work stems from creating these metrics, which offer a novel approach to examining and interpreting biological systems. By incorporating principles from physics, like Bose-Einstein condensation, into biology, we provide a new viewpoint for analyzing population dynamics and species interactions. Our findings contribute to the broader understanding of how biological systems evolve and adapt, with potential implications for ecology and conservation efforts.

We initiated our study with a Grey Literature Review (GLR) to establish an initial understanding of the strategies employed by practitioners to manage flaky tests. This review serves as the basis for our upcoming mitigation analysis and guides the development of our interviews. Our GLR is exploratory and non-exhaustive, aiming to map the existing mitigation measures. We followed recognized guidelines for performing a systematic review, concentrating on resources that describe practitioners' experiences and approaches in tackling flakiness, including technical reports, presentations, and blogs. Our search approach generated 276,000 results, which were filtered down to 100 articles via an optimized Google search query. We meticulously selected 56 articles written by practitioners that provided practical insights into flakiness mitigation, excluding theoretical discussions and research articles. In our analysis, we applied a quality assessment checklist to ensure the relevance and reliability of the selected articles. We identified three critical exclusion criteria: objectivity, method adequacy, and topic adequacy, which helped us to refine our selection to 38 articles. Using a consensus-based approach, we developed a classification of the mitigation strategies outlined by practitioners, as presented in Table~\ref{table:strategies} and elaborated in Section~\ref{sec:results}. Our GLR revealed a significant gap in the literature regarding the rationale behind the choice of mitigation measures and their consequences, which our interview process aimed to address. Furthermore, our study's implications suggest future work in leveraging monitoring and log analysis, establishing testing guidelines, and developing tools for root cause identification and reproduction of flaky tests. These insights open avenues for research that could assist practitioners in managing flakiness more effectively. Our introduction presents the essential function of software testing in contemporary development and the difficulties introduced by flaky tests, which may diminish developers' confidence in test suites and affect software quality. We highlight the prevalence and cost of flaky tests in large software systems, citing Google's experience with over 50 million test cases executed daily and the significant budget allocated to managing flaky tests. Our study builds on previous empirical research by examining the industrial context of flakiness and conducting qualitative analyses based on 14 practitioner interviews. By employing this method, we seek to uncover the common actions practitioners take and investigate how research-based solutions might improve these practices. Our study is guided by research questions that examine the localization of flakiness, how practitioners view its effects, and the methods they use to address it.

This section presents a new method for selecting variables in high-dimensional datasets, utilizing the harmonic mean p-value along with an improved strategy for choosing tuning parameters. The proposed method transcends the limitations of traditional approaches, such as Fisher’s method, by not requiring the assumption of independence among p-values. We utilize p-values to develop an estimator, $\hat{\pi}$, which estimates the proportion of non-zero variables, a key consideration for improving the selection of the tuning parameter, $\lambda$, in penalized regression techniques. Specifically, we suggest a data-driven method to determine a narrower and more efficient tuning range for $\lambda$, based on the estimated proportion of non-zero variables, $\hat{\pi}p$. This approach is illustrated via a Lasso solution path and cross-validation curve, showing a substantial decrease in the $\lambda$ search space and resulting in a more precise model selection. The innovative contributions of this research are manifold: 1. The incorporation of a harmonic mean p-value that reduces the requirement for independence among p-values, thus expanding the method's applicability. 2. The development of a novel estimator, \(\hat{\pi}\), that provides a more nuanced understanding of the underlying variable structure in high-dimensional data. 3. The proposition of a refined tuning region for \(\lambda\) that is both data-driven and theoretically justified, leading to enhanced model selection in penalized regression methods. Our findings are substantiated through rigorous simulation studies that compare the performance of Lasso, adaptive Lasso, SCAD, and MCP under varying signal strengths and block dependence structures. The results underscore the superiority of our approach in terms of true positive rate, false positive rate, and overall model accuracy, as measured by diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) and F1 score. The simulation studies not only confirm the theoretical improvements but also offer empirical support for the practical effectiveness of our method in variable selection tasks.

We introduce a new framework for examining the structure of vector spaces and algebras over a quotient field, concentrating on the characteristics of matrices and their transformations in this setting. Our method is based on the idea of a vector space $ V $ over the quotient field $ \tilde{K} $ of a domain $ K $, along with the dimension $ n $ of $ V_{\tilde{K}} $. By leveraging the non-zero element \( P_{11} \), we construct a basis \( B_{1} \) for \( V_{\tilde{K}} \) and demonstrate that the matrices \( f_{1}(P_{ij}) \) have rank 1 over \( K \). This insight allows us to decompose these matrices into products of matrices \( A \) and \( B \), leading to the key result \( BA = I \), which simplifies the analysis of the matrix transformations. Our research presents a method for expressing elements $ P_{ij} $ as elementary matrices within a particular basis $ B_{3} $ of the module $ V $ over $ K $. This representation is pivotal in understanding the underlying algebraic structure and its implications for the study of algebraic varieties and their automorphisms. In the realm of homogeneous varieties of algebras, we delve into the properties of the T-ideal and its implications for the structure of the variety. We demonstrate that certain varieties, such as associative, nilpotent, Lie, alternative, and Jordan algebras, are homogeneous, and we explore the decomposition of free algebras in these varieties. A key result is the lemma that any endomorphism \( \varphi \) of \( F \) maps \( F' \) into itself, which is instrumental in our subsequent analysis. Our main proposition states that for a homogeneous variety $ \Theta $ of linear algebras over an R$_{1}$MF-domain $ K $, if $ \Theta $ is contained within either the variety of linear algebras defined by $ x_{1}^{2} = 0 $ or the variety of nilpotent algebras of class $ \leq m $, then every automorphism of the semigroup $ End\,F $ is quasi-inner. The proof involves a detailed examination of the matrices representing the endomorphisms and their properties, leading to the conclusion that the automorphisms can be represented as conjugations by elementary matrices. We further illustrate the application of our findings with an example of a variety of linear algebras over a Dedekind domain, where we construct a non-quasi-inner automorphism of the endomorphism semigroup, highlighting the boundaries of our main proposition. Our work contributes to the field by providing a deeper understanding of the algebraic structures over quotient fields and their automorphisms, with potential implications for further research in algebraic varieties and their applications.

Cheesemakers have a long history of using colorants to enhance the appearance of their products. In times past, farmers would sometimes produce milk of lesser quality, which would result in a whiter cheese. To make this cheese more appealing to consumers, they began adding colorants to mimic the richer hues of higher-quality summer cheeses. Initially, these colorants were derived from natural sources such as saffron, marigold, and carrot juice. However, in the 17th century, the Dutch introduced a new colorant known as annatto. The Dutch had established colonies in Guyana and traded food, including annatto, with the indigenous communities. Zeeland merchants, operating under the West India Company, acquired annatto from the coastal areas of Guyana and Suriname and marketed it in the Netherlands as "verw," meaning "paint." The earliest documented instance of annatto's application in cheese production is noted from 1743, as mentioned in the Dutch publication "Huishoudelyk Woordboek" (Household Dictionary), per American scholar Paul Kindstedt from the University of Vermont. Other historical documents from the same period confirm that the use of annatto, also referred to as "orleaan" or "orleans," to color cheese was already in practice by the mid-18th century. Another nation with a documented tradition of employing annatto for cheese coloring is England. As early as the 16th century, colorants were added to Gloucester cheese to allow inferior cheese to be passed off as the superior Double Gloucester variety. Annatto was later adopted for this purpose as well. In summary, the use of colorants in cheese production has been a common practice for centuries, with annatto emerging as a popular choice due to its vibrant orange-red hue. This method enabled cheesemakers to enhance the appearance of their cheeses and, in certain instances, mislead consumers into thinking they were buying a superior product.

This study examines the environmental effects on the activity of star-forming galaxies throughout various cosmic times, concentrating on the connection between stellar mass ($M_*$), star formation rate (SFR), and the deviation from the main sequence. Our analysis reveals no significant environmental differences at any of the three considered epochs, suggesting that the star-forming activity of galaxies in clusters and the field follows similar evolutionary paths. Notably, at redshift $z=2.2$, a mild indication suggests that cluster galaxies might possess greater stellar masses and SFRs, aligning with earlier research emphasizing enhanced galaxy development in proto-cluster settings during the initial stages of cluster formation. The specific star formation rate (SSFR) of H$\alpha$-selected galaxies in both cluster and field environments shows a significant decrease with redshift, adhering to a trend of roughly $(1+z)^3$ starting from $z\sim 2$. This decline aligns well with the broader understanding of the cosmic star formation history. Our findings support the notion that star-forming galaxies in cluster environments have been evolving similarly to those in the general field, at least when considering SFRs derived from H$\alpha$ emissions. Our results contribute to the ongoing debate on the environmental dependence of galaxy star formation in the distant Universe. While some studies suggest a higher SFR in high-density environments, others indicate a weak or absent correlation between SSFR and environmental density. Our study contributes to the growing evidence indicating that the SFR--$M_*$ relationship for star-forming galaxies does not show a strong environmental dependence since $z\sim 2$. However, the potential influence of AGNs on our findings warrants further investigation. While the majority of our H$\alpha$-selected galaxies are probably driven by star formation, it is still possible that AGN contributions might differ depending on redshift, mass, and environmental factors, which could affect our results. Future detailed studies, including spectroscopy, are necessary to clarify the role of AGNs in the observed star formation activity. In summary, our research provides a robust comparison of star-forming galaxies in cluster and field environments, highlighting the consistent evolution of these galaxies across cosmic time. Our results underscore the importance of additional study regarding the impact of AGNs and the subtleties of environmental effects on star formation.

Conifers and grasses are known for producing lightweight pollen, which is primarily dispersed by the wind to neighboring plants. This method of pollination is known as anemophily. In contrast, certain flowering plants have developed to generate heavier, sticky pollen that is specially adapted for transport by insects or larger animals. These pollinators, including hummingbirds and bats, are frequently drawn to flowers that provide nectar and pollen as incentives. As these animals move from one flower to another, they inadvertently transport pollen, leading to pollination. This process is known as entomophily. Fungi, on the other hand, have a diverse range of reproductive strategies. Most species of fungi can reproduce sexually, and their life cycles involve both haploid and diploid phases. These fungi are typically isogamous, meaning they do not exhibit male and female specialization. Instead, one haploid fungus grows into contact with another, and they fuse their cells. In some instances, the fusion may be asymmetric, with one cell donating only a nucleus, which could be considered a male role. Fungi may also possess more complex mating systems with additional sexes that do not fit the traditional male, female, or hermaphroditic classifications. Some fungi, such as baker's yeast, have mating types that determine compatibility. Yeasts with the same mating types will not fuse to form diploid cells; only those with different mating types will do so. Many higher fungi produce mushrooms as part of their sexual reproduction process. Within the mushroom, diploid cells are formed, which later divide into haploid spores. A sexual system refers to the distribution of male and female reproductive structures within a species. This can vary widely across different organisms, from separate male and female individuals (dioecious) to hermaphroditic individuals that possess both male and female reproductive organs (monoecious). Studying the sexual systems of different organisms is essential for examining their reproductive biology, ecology, and evolutionary aspects.

\section*{Keywords} Stochastic dynamical systems, Neuronal network modeling, Asymptotic analysis, WKB approximation, Eikonal equations, Attractor escape. \section*{AMS classification} 37A50, 60G40, 92B25, 41A60 \section{Introduction} In this study, we delve into the intricate dynamics of stochastic dynamical systems, particularly focusing on the role of small noise perturbations. These perturbations can significantly alter system trajectories, enabling escape from stable attractor basins and inducing phenomena such as stochastic resonance and bifurcation shifts \cite{dykman1994observable, dykman1994large, maier1993, lindner2004, schimanskyGeier1985, arnold1979, arnold1990, Wihstutz_book2003}. Our research is particularly relevant in the context of biological neuronal networks, where noise is crucial for collective rhythms and synchronization \cite{Tsodyks1997, BrunelHakim1999, Hansel2001, Holcman_Tsodyks2006, Barak2007, daoduc2015}. We introduce a reduced stochastic dynamical system based on synaptic depression-facilitation, a model that captures the essence of neuronal network bursting activity \cite{Tsodyks1997, daoduc2015}. Our approach involves analyzing the distribution of interburst intervals, which correspond to escapes from an attractor. We reveal that the escape rate and the distribution of exit points can be determined using the WKB approximation, a method that provides insights into the small noise limit \cite{Matkowsky1977exit, Schuss:Book, Schuss1980, BobrovskySchuss1982}. Our study advances knowledge about escape dynamics in periodically-driven systems, with the escape rate dependent on the field strength \cite{smelyanskiy1999time, dykman2005}. We highlight the distinction between exiting and escaping, a clarification that is crucial for our analysis. The manuscript is structured to first present our reduced stochastic model, followed by an exploration of a generic two-dimensional dynamical system containing an attractor and a saddle-point. We demonstrate that the maximum of the probability density function of trajectories before escape is shifted, depending on the noise amplitude $\sigma$. Our analysis culminates in an examination of the escape from the basin of attraction, where trajectories can reenter the basin multiple times before final escape, a phenomenon that has implications for the large tail distribution of interburst intervals observed in experimental data \cite{Rouach_CxKO}. \section{Modeling the Interburst Durations in Neuronal Networks} \subsection{Noisy Depression-Facilitation Model} Neuronal networks exhibit complex activity patterns, which can be modeled using mean-field models to represent the dynamics as stochastic differential equations. Bursting dynamics, characterized by transient periods of neuronal discharge, can be understood through the lens of short-term synaptic plasticity properties such as depression and facilitation \cite{Tsodyks1997, Barak2007, daoduc2015}. These properties are crucial for understanding the interburst periods, during which the network is relatively inactive. We focus on a depression-facilitation short-term synaptic plasticity model that describes network neuronal bursting \cite{Tsodyks1997, daoduc2015frontiers, Holcman_Tsodyks2006}. This model is represented by three equations for the mean voltage $h$, the depression $y$, and the facilitation $x$. The model incorporates the return to equilibrium, the increase in vesicular release probability, and the depletion of vesicular pools, all of which are essential for understanding the network activity. \subsection{Reduction to a Two-Dimensional System and Phase-Space Analysis} The system under consideration has three critical points: one attractor and two saddle-points. By reducing the system to a 2D-plane, we simplify the analysis while retaining the essential dynamics. The deterministic system, when reduced, has two attractors and one saddle-point. Our analysis reveals that the attractor's dynamics are anisotropic, with the eigenvalues indicating the stability and nature of the critical points. The escape dynamics from the attractor basin are characterized by trajectories that can reenter the basin multiple times before eventually escaping to infinity. This behavior is distinct from systems where escape ends upon the first encounter with the separatrix. Our study provides a novel explanation for the observed large tail distribution of interburst intervals in experimental time series, suggesting that each excursion outside and inside the basin of attraction contributes to an increased total escape time.

In this section, we present the Group-Sort-Fuse (GSF) method, a new penalized maximum likelihood technique for determining the order and components of a finite mixture model. Given a random sample from an unknown true mixing measure \( G_0 \) with at most \( K_0 \) components, we propose a method to address overfitting issues associated with the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) when an upper bound \( K \geq K_0 \) is known. The overfitted MLE may converge slowly and include superfluous components, leading to an inconsistent estimate of \( K_0 \). Our GSF approach incorporates two kinds of penalties to address these problems: one aimed at suppressing near-zero mixing probabilities and another designed to combine closely situated estimated atoms. We first introduce a preliminary penalized log-likelihood function that incorporates a nonnegative penalty $ \varphi $ to guarantee that the maximizer has mixing probabilities bounded away from zero, resulting in a consistent estimator of the atoms of $ G_0 $. However, this initial estimator fails to consistently estimate the order $ K_0 $ because it does not account for the second type of overfitting. To tackle this issue, we propose a sparsity-inducing penalty $ r_{\lambda_n} $ applied to the distances between selected pairs of atoms, concentrating on their consecutive distances following a sorting process, instead of considering all pairwise distances, thereby decreasing dependence on the selection of $ K $. The GSF method is based on the idea of cluster partitioning, in which atoms are organized into clusters with the property that distances inside clusters are less than those between different clusters. The method aims to merge estimates within each cluster to approximate the true atoms of \( G_0 \). To achieve this, we define a cluster ordering, a permutation of atoms that respects the cluster partition and is invariant to relabeling. The GSF method then fuses the ordered atoms within each cluster to produce a consistent estimator of both the order and components of the true mixing measure. The key contributions of our research encompass the introduction of a doubly penalized log-likelihood function that efficiently mitigates overfitting in mixture models, the creation of a cluster partitioning approach that improves the estimation of genuine components, and the application of cluster ordering to combine nearby atoms. Our method provides a significant advancement in the field of mixture model estimation, offering a more accurate and robust approach to estimating the underlying structure of the data.

Reverse Reverb is a sound effect that has been utilized in various music genres and media productions. It involves the application of reverb in reverse, creating a unique and ethereal sound. This technique has been employed by numerous artists and bands over the years, contributing to the distinctiveness of their music. One of the first documented instances of reverse reverb dates to the song "Whole Lotta Love" by Led Zeppelin, which was released in 1969. The effect was used in the bridge of the song, adding a haunting quality to the music. Another early example is found in "Alucard" from Gentle Giant's self-titled album, which was released in 1970. Throughout the 1970s, the use of reverse reverb became somewhat common, as seen in "Crying to the Sky" by Be-Bop Deluxe. In the realm of shoegaze music, reverse reverb is a popular technique, particularly among bands like My Bloody Valentine and Spacemen 3. This effect is frequently employed to produce a dreamlike, ambient quality that defines the genre. Additionally, reverse reverb has found its way into hardstyle music, electronic dance music (EDM), and pop music, where it is commonly applied to the first word or syllable of a vocal passage. This technique serves as a lead-in to vocal sections, creating a build-up effect or an other-worldly sound. Notable instances of reverse reverb in popular music feature Metallica's application of the effect on James Hetfield's vocals in the track "Fade To Black" from their 1984 album "Ride The Lightning." Likewise, Genesis incorporated the effect on Phil Collins' snare drum towards the conclusion of the song "Deep in the Motherload" from their 1978 album "And Then There Three." Additionally, reverse reverb has found applications beyond music, appearing in fields like film and television production. It is often utilized to create an otherworldly effect on voices, particularly in horror movies, where it can add a sense of eeriness and suspense. Additionally, the effect has been used in the company logo for production company CBS Studios, demonstrating its versatility and impact in various forms of media. In summary, reverse reverb is a sound effect that has been embraced by musicians and media producers alike, adding a unique and captivating quality to their work. Its use in various genres and media formats showcases the creative potential of this technique and its enduring appeal in the world of sound design.

Oral administration involves the delivery of substances, such as medications, into the mouth, which are then swallowed and processed via the digestive system. It is a widely used route for various drugs due to its ease of use and relatively painless nature compared to other methods like injections. However, the effectiveness of orally administered medications can be influenced by factors such as proper absorption in the digestive system and potential breakdown by digestive enzymes before reaching the bloodstream. Additionally, some medications may cause gastrointestinal side effects, including nausea or vomiting. Oral administration is suitable for conscious patients who are able to swallow. The phrase "per os," originating from Latin, means "through the mouth" or "by mouth" and is employed in medical terminology to refer to medications administered orally. The abbreviation "P.O." is frequently seen on medical prescriptions to denote oral intake. Enteral delivery, which is a type of oral delivery, includes various approaches: 1. Buccal: The medication is dissolved inside the cheek. 2. Sublabial: The drug is dissolved beneath the lip. 3. Sublingual administration (SL): The medication is dissolved under the tongue. Due to rapid absorption, some consider SL a parenteral route. 4. Oral (PO): The medication is taken as a swallowed tablet, capsule, or liquid. Enteral medications come in different forms, such as oral solid dosage (OSD) forms, which include tablets intended to be swallowed, chewed, dissolved in water, or placed under the tongue. It is essential to follow the specific instructions provided with each medication to ensure optimal effectiveness and minimize potential side effects.

Universal quantification and existential quantification are key concepts in first-order logic, a foundational system for mathematical reasoning. These concepts were notably discussed by Thoralf Skolem, who introduced the notion of a "definite property." According to van Heijenoort, a property is considered definite in Skolem's sense if it can be expressed by a well-formed formula in the simple predicate calculus of first order, where the only predicate constants are epsilon (ε) and possibly equality (=). In modern set theory, axiomatizations are typically embedded within a logical calculus framework. The formulation of the axiom of separation, which is crucial for defining subsets, is largely influenced by the approaches of Hermann Weyl and Skolem. It is essential to recognize a transition in terminology from "propositional function" to expressions such as "formula," "predicate calculus," "predicate," and "logical calculus." This transition is further detailed in sections that address the notion of "function" within modern set theory. The history of the "ordered pair" concept is somewhat unclear. In 1879, Gottlob Frege introduced an intuitive ordering within his definition of a two-argument function Ψ(A, B). Norbert Wiener, in his 1914 work, recognized that his approach essentially returned to Ernst Schröder's method of considering a relation as a set of ordered pairs. Bertrand Russell, in 1903, proposed defining a relation as a "class of couples" but eventually dismissed this notion, claiming that it sidestepped the need for a more detailed comprehension of relations. In summary, the development of set theory and the logical underpinnings of mathematical reasoning have been shaped by the contributions of various mathematicians and logicians. The evolution of terminology and the exploration of foundational concepts, such as ordered pairs and definite properties, have played a significant role in the advancement of these fields.

This section introduces the methodology for estimating the parameters of the HIV transmission model using Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC). The Nadaraya-Watson regression estimator is used to estimate the mean of the target distribution, along with additional statistics like medians, modes, and credibility intervals being calculated. The Cuban HIV-AIDS dataset, covering the period from 1986 to 2007, is utilized for analysis, with summary statistics obtained from the detection times and methods used for detection. A comparison of ABC and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods is provided for a standard SIR model, illustrating ABC's capacity to reproduce likelihood-based outcomes under suitable conditions. The impact of tolerance rate on the posterior distribution is discussed, highlighting the tendency of ABC to produce larger tails compared to MCMC. The paper also addresses the challenge of the "curse of dimensionality" in ABC, where the bias may increase with the number of summary statistics. Regression-based approaches are suggested to alleviate this problem, such as local linear regressions and nonlinear conditional heteroscedastic regressions, with the goal of establishing a link between the distributions and reducing the parameter estimates towards an approximate sample from the target distribution. The innovative aspects of this research include the application of ABC to the HIV transmission model, the comparison with MCMC methods, and the introduction of regression adjustments to address the curse of dimensionality. The results enhance insight into parameter estimation within intricate models where direct likelihood-based inference proves difficult.

This section delves into the competitive dynamics that characterize Wikipedia's collaborative content creation process, where contributors often vie for ownership of the content they produce. We draw on psychological ownership theory and territoriality theory to explain why contributors may develop a sense of ownership over Wikipedia articles or sections thereof, leading to competition and potential conflicts over the direction and content of these articles. Wikipedia's governance model, which is based on community-developed norms and policies, plays a critical role in mitigating these competitive tendencies. The Neutral Point of View (NPOV) principle is central to this model, promoting objectivity and preventing any single viewpoint from dominating an article. However, achieving NPOV can be challenging due to the complexity of issues, difficulty in verifying information, and intentional attempts by contributors to influence readers' perspectives. Our study seeks to examine the interaction between competitive forces and socio-technical governance structures within Wikipedia's peer-production framework. We concentrate on two research questions: Firstly, how do contributors weigh the costs and benefits of peer-production, and what is the connection between their editing activities and fractional ownership of articles? Second, how do governance mechanisms, particularly the enforcement of NPOV, affect the competitive dynamics and the relationship between contributors' editing efforts and content ownership? We propose a game-theoretic model to analyze competition and governance in Wikipedia's co-production process. This model aims to represent the key characteristics of the system, taking into account both cooperative and competitive actions, and offer understanding of the intricate relationships among contributors and the community's governance structures. Our study's innovative aspects lie in examining the competitive dynamics within Wikipedia's collaborative environment and understanding how these dynamics are influenced by the community's governance efforts, particularly in relation to the NPOV principle. By doing so, we aim to contribute to the literature on peer production and the socio-technical systems that underpin it.

This study introduces a novel Bayesian spatio-temporal approach to analyze respiratory prescription data at the General Practitioner (GP) surgery level in Scotland from 2015 to 2016. Respiratory prescriptions make up 13% of the total cost of all prescriptions in Scotland, highlighting the importance of examining the factors that affect their distribution and the spatial variations in prescription rates. The data's distinctive feature of being point-level with fixed locations, where forecasting at unobserved locations is not possible, presented a challenge. To address this, we proposed a finite dimensional process-convolution model that does not presuppose an underlying spatial process that is universally measurable. Our approach enhances current process-convolution models by integrating an adaptive or localized spatial structure via a tapered random weighting method. We provide open-source software to ensure the research is reproducible. The adaptive model significantly outperforms a simpler global smoothing model, leading to two principal findings. First, we establish a positive association between respiratory prescription rates and air pollution, particularly PM2.5. A rise of 1.23 µg/m³ in PM2.5 corresponds to a 2.2% increase in prescription rates. This finding is consistent with existing literature that associates air pollution with more severe health outcomes, such as hospitalization or death, and reinforces the evidence that air pollution significantly impacts respiratory health and associated healthcare costs, even at concentrations below legal limits. The study also highlights significant disparities in respiratory prescription rates across different Scottish health boards. Dumfries and Galloway, along with Greater Glasgow and Clyde, have the highest rates, showing increases of 27% and 19% respectively when compared to the Scottish average. In contrast, Grampian and Orkney exhibit the lowest rates, experiencing reductions of 30% and 40% respectively. These differences remain apparent both prior to and following adjustment for recognized covariates, suggesting a notable residual impact of health boards on respiratory prescription rates. These results are vital for informing public health policy and resource allocation discussions, particularly in the context of ongoing debates sparked by the Marmot review in England and recent reports highlighting health inequalities. The study also opens avenues for future research, including the development of a multivariate extension of the model to explore inter-relationships between prescribing rates for different diseases and the creation of interactive software for data visualization to better communicate health inequalities to policymakers.

We propose an innovative approach to estimate the quantity \(\psi(P)\), which is dependent on the tail of a probability distribution \(P\). Instead of fitting \(P\) to a parametric distribution, we introduce an optimization problem that imposes a geometric shape condition on the tail of \(P\), defined by \(x \geq a\) for a sufficiently large threshold \(a\). This method ensures consistent extrapolation from the non-tail region and incorporates auxiliary constraints to provide additional information about \(P\). The optimization problem is designed to deliver an upper confidence bound for \(\psi(P)\), supported by a statistical guarantee that if the constraints hold for the true distribution \(P_{\text{true}}\) with a confidence level of \(1-\alpha\), then the optimal value \(Z^*\) is an upper confidence bound for the true value \(Z_{\text{true}}\) with at least the same confidence level. Our approach focuses on \(\psi(P)\) that represents either an expectation or a quantile of a random variable \(X\). We impose geometric conditions such as monotonicity and convexity on the tail of \(P\), which are common to most parametric distributions. These conditions come with distributional information at the threshold $a$, functioning as boundary conditions to enable natural extrapolation and prevent the optimization from becoming trivial. The auxiliary constraints, in the form of moment conditions, are calibrated using data and help reduce the conservativeness of the extrapolation. The optimization problem can be expressed as: \[ \begin{aligned} \max_P \quad & \psi(P) \\ \text{subject to} \quad & P \in \mathscr{P}, \quad \mathbb{E}_P[\bm{g}(X)] \in \mathbb{S} \end{aligned} \] where \(\mathscr{P}\) represents the set of distributions satisfying the geometric shape conditions, and \(\mathbb{S}\) represents the set of permissible moment conditions. The feasible region for this problem is represented by $\mathbb F(\mathfrak{P}(\mathscr{P},\bm{g},\mathbb{S}))$. Our approach introduces a novel aspect through its capacity to ensure statistical validity for the estimated parameter $\psi(P)$, even under limited knowledge regarding the distribution's tail behavior. By combining geometric shape conditions with auxiliary moment constraints, we offer a robust framework for tail-related estimation problems. This method proves especially beneficial in situations where conventional parametric fitting might not be suitable or when analyzing the tail characteristics of the distribution is the main focus.

In this paper, we examine the complex interactions of mean curvature flow, a foundational mechanism in geometric evolution, specifically within the framework of symmetric spaces. We start by presenting the idea of a mean curvature flow, defined as a one-parameter family of immersions that deforms a manifold according to its mean curvature vector. Our focus is on the evolution of submanifolds, specifically equifocal and proper complex equifocal submanifolds, which are generalizations of isoparametric submanifolds in Euclidean spaces to the more complex structure of symmetric spaces. Our research is based on prior work by Liu-Terng and Terng-Thorbergsson, who examined the dynamics of mean curvature flows initiated with isoparametric and equifocal submanifolds in Euclidean and compact symmetric spaces, respectively. These studies revealed intriguing properties, such as the collapse of submanifolds to focal submanifolds and the existence of singularities under certain conditions. Building upon these ideas, we present the concept of a proper complex equifocal submanifold within a symmetric space of non-compact type, defined by its complex focal configuration and the influence of a symmetric subgroup. We highlight the importance of curvature-adapted submanifolds, which are those that align with the curvature of the ambient space, and their role as principal orbits in Hermann type actions. Our main contribution lies in the formulation and proof of a theorem that addresses the behavior of mean curvature flows with curvature-adapted proper complex equifocal submanifolds or their focal submanifolds as initial data in non-compact symmetric spaces, excluding hyperbolic spaces. This theorem broadens the comprehension of how submanifolds evolve geometrically under mean curvature flow and offers a more profound understanding of the relationship between submanifold geometry and the curvature of the surrounding space. In summary, our paper presents a comprehensive exploration of the mean curvature flow of complex equifocal submanifolds in symmetric spaces, offering new perspectives on their geometric evolution and the underlying principles governing their behavior. Through rigorous mathematical analysis, we contribute to the field by elucidating the complex dynamics at play and setting the stage for further research in this area.

A prescription serves as a written directive issued by a qualified healthcare practitioner, like a doctor or dentist, granting permission to a patient for obtaining a particular medication. It typically includes various legal requirements, such as a registration number, for example, a DEA (Drug Enforcement Administration) Number in the United States. Each prescription is unique to the patient and contains the patient's name. In the United Kingdom and Ireland, the patient's name and address are also required. The prescription is dated, and some jurisdictions may impose a time limit on its validity. In the past, prescriptions provided directions for pharmacists to prepare pharmaceutical compounds. However, most modern prescriptions specify pre-manufactured pharmaceutical products that require minimal or no preparation by the pharmacist. The directions for the patient to follow when taking the medication are printed on the label of the pharmaceutical product. The term "prescription" originates from the Latin words "pre-" (meaning "before") and "script" (meaning "writing" or "written"). This reflects the fact that a prescription is an order that must be documented before a drug can be dispensed. In the industry, prescriptions are often colloquially referred to as "scripts." A prescription typically contains the following information: - The healthcare professional who prescribed the medication - The patient for whom the prescription is valid - The specific pharmaceutical product prescribed In some cases, additional information may be required depending on the jurisdiction, type of drug, or patient group. For instance, many brand-name drugs have cheaper generic alternatives that are therapeutically and biochemically equivalent. Prescriptions might also contain directions regarding whether the prescriber allows replacement with a generic alternative. In summary, a prescription is a crucial document that ensures patients receive the appropriate medication as directed by a healthcare professional. It contains essential information and may include specific instructions regarding drug equivalence and substitution.

Induction motors are known for their significant reactive component, which results in a low power factor. This low power factor causes an increase in reactive current taken from the power supply, resulting in extra losses within the power system. To address this problem, synchronous motors can be used in industrial facilities to provide the required reactive power for induction motors. This method improves the total power factor of the plant and decreases the reactive current taken from the grid. Synchronous motors designed for power factor correction are known as synchronous condensers. They offer seamless, automatic power factor correction and can generate up to 150% additional reactive power (vars). These devices remain unaffected by electrical harmonics within the system and may, in certain instances, also absorb them. Synchronous condensers do not produce switching transients, excessive voltage levels, or electrical resonances. The rotational inertia of a synchronous condenser enables it to offer restricted voltage assistance during short-term power interruptions. Introduced in the 1930s and widely used in the 1950s, synchronous condensers were eventually replaced by static var compensators (SVCs) in new installations due to their higher costs. However, they continue to serve as a feasible alternative or complement to capacitors for power factor correction, particularly in cases where harmonics have led to capacitor overheating and malfunctions. Synchronous condensers can also be advantageous in maintaining voltage levels. The reactive power provided by a capacitor bank is directly proportional to the square of its terminal voltage. This relationship highlights the importance of maintaining appropriate voltage levels for optimal performance and efficiency in power systems.

This section introduces the formulation of Convolutional Kernel Networks (CKNs) and their connection to traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets). CKNs are infinite-dimensional analogues of ConvNets, utilizing kernel functions to capture spatial relationships in data. The central hyperparameter in CKNs is the selection of kernel, which conventionally adopts a normalized form based on a dot product kernel on the sphere. This selection enables the confinement of filters to the sphere, requiring a projection step during the optimization process. The representation at every layer within a CKN is formed by a sequence of operations such as patch extraction, normalization, projection, and pooling. Following multiple layers, a final representation appropriate for classification tasks is achieved. The optimization problem for training CKNs involves minimizing a loss function subject to constraints that the filters lie on a product of Euclidean spheres. A crucial feature of CKNs lies in their alignment with ConvNet elements, as outlined in Table~\ref{tab:correspondence}. This table illustrates the analogous components within CKNs corresponding to various layers and operations in ConvNets, including convolutional layers, partially connected layers, and pooling. The proposition presented formalizes the connection between the pointwise nonlinearity in ConvNets and the approximation of a kernel on patches. The section further explores the details of how various layer types in ConvNets, including convolutional, partially-connected, and fully connected layers, correspond to CKNs through subspace projections. It also covers the idea of pooling in ConvNets and its equivalent to averaging feature maps in CKNs. Additionally, the normalization techniques prevalent in ConvNets, such as local response normalization, are examined in the context of CKNs. The innovative aspect of this research lies in the detailed exploration of the relationship between CKNs and ConvNets, providing insights into how the traditional finite-dimensional ConvNet operations can be generalized to the infinite-dimensional CKN framework. This comprehension may enable the development of more efficient and effective network architectures by utilizing the strong representational capabilities of kernel methods.

This section provides a thorough mathematical examination of the large deviations principle (LDP) for empirical measures within the framework of mean-field games. We establish the LDP by leveraging the contraction principle, which allows us to transfer the LDP from empirical measures of initial states and noise variables to the state-action empirical measures. The main result is encapsulated in Theorem \ref{theorem3}, which characterizes the rate function for the LDP in terms of the game dynamics. Our approach begins by proving that the bounded function $h_f^{k+1}$ is continuous for all its arguments except noise variables, which is crucial for the induction argument. This continuity is then used to establish the weak convergence of the empirical measures to the true measures for each $t\geq0$. The proof is concluded by employing the contraction principle, which provides the LDP for the empirical measures. In Theorem \ref{theorem3}, the rate function $J$ is expressed in terms of the noise distributions $\Theta_w$ and $\Theta_v$. However, these distributions may not always be known. To address this, we derive an equivalent rate function that can be expressed solely in terms of the components of the game dynamics. This is achieved by using the chain rule for relative entropy and redefining the rate function $J$ in terms of the empirical measure $ u_{0,{\mathsf X}}$ and the relative entropy with respect to the product measure $ u_{0,{\mathsf X}}\times\Theta_w\times\Theta_v$. We then introduce a simplified particle model to further analyze the rate function. This model decouples the agents and replaces the empirical measure of states with a fixed measure in the state dynamics. By utilizing Sanov's Theorem along with the contraction principle, we derive the LDP for the empirical measures of this simplified model, with a rate function $\tilde{J}$. The connection between the rate functions $J$ and $\tilde{J}$ is established through Lemma \ref{lemma3}, which shows that the sets of measures that map to a given empirical measure under $\Phi$ and $\Phi^{{\boldsymbol u}}$ are the same. This allows us to express $J$ as the sum of the relative entropy with respect to the initial measure and the rate function $\tilde{J}$. Finally, we offer a description of the rate function $\tilde{J}$ based on the game dynamics, resulting in the final formula for $J$ presented in Theorem \ref{theorem2}. This result is obtained by considering the empirical measures of the paths and applying Sanov's Theorem in the weak convergence topology. In conclusion, this section presents a comprehensive analysis of the LDP for empirical measures in mean-field games, providing a deeper understanding of the behavior of these measures under the mean-field equilibrium policy. The results have potential applications in various fields, such as economics, finance, and social sciences, where understanding the dynamics of large populations is crucial. Future research directions could include studying concentration bounds for these empirical measures and exploring the implications of the LDP in different contexts.

This article examines a $p$-adic analysis of a minimal degree differential algebraic equation which annihilates an arithmetic Gevrey series of order $-1$, namely an $E$-function. We confirm a conjecture proposed by Yves Andr\'e (Conjecture 4.7 of [A2]). At the outset, we establish certain notations. Let $K$ be a number field and $V_{0}$ the collection of all finite places $v$ of $K$. For each $v \in V_{0}$ above a prime number $p = p(v)$, we normalize the $v$-adic absolute value such that $|p|_{v} = p^{-1}$ and denote $\pi_{v} = p^{\frac{-1}{p-1}}$. Let $K_{v}$ be the completion of $K$ for this absolute value, and fix an embedding $K \hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}$. For any real number $r > 0$, the \emph{generic convergence radius} $R_{v}(\phi, r)$ of a differential operator $\displaystyle\phi \in K[x, d/dx]$ is defined as the convergence radius, upper bounded by $r$, of a solution base of $\phi$ near a generic $v$-adic point of absolute value $r$. A formal power series $\sum_{n\ge 0}a_nx^n$ is called an \emph{arithmetic Gevrey series} of order $s \in \mathbb{Q}$ if its coefficients $a_n$ are algebraic numbers and there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that the algebraic numbers $a_n/(n!)^s$ have conjugates with absolute value less than $C^n$, and for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the common denominator $d_n$ of the numbers $a_0/(0!)^s, \ This class encompasses generalized convergent or divergent hypergeometric series featuring rational parameters. The set of such series is denoted by $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\{x\}_s$. A formal series having algebraic coefficients is termed holonomic when it satisfies a linear differential equation with coefficients in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(x)$. The $G$-functions (resp. $E$-functions) are defined as the holonomic elements of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\{x\}_0$ (resp. $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\{x\}_{-1}$). The theory of $G$-functions has experienced significant expansion in recent decades, mainly as a result of the research conducted by Chudnovsky, Bombieri, and Andr\'e. Their contributions have highlighted certain connections with transcendence and arithmetic geometry. In particular, Chudnovsky proved that the differential operator $\phi$ of $K[x, d/dx]$ of minimal order in $d/dx$ annihilating a $G$-function satisfies the so-called Galochkin condition (cf. [CC], [A1, VI]). A differential operator of $K[x, d/dx]$ fulfilling this condition is called a \emph{$G$-operator}. Andr\'e later established the equivalence between this condition and that of Bombieri, that is, a differential operator $\phi$ of $K[x, d/dx]$ is a $G$-operator if and only if it satisfies $\prod_{v\in V_0}R_{v}(\phi,1) e 0$ [A1, IV 5.2]. Thanks to Katz's theorem [Ka, 13.0], we confirm that $G$-operators possess only regular singularities with rational exponents. Moreover, all formal series involved in their solutions, at any finite or infinite point, are $G$-functions [A1, V]. The study of non-zero order holonomic arithmetic Gevrey series has been recently developed by Y. Andr\'e in [A2]. In particular, he introduced a new class of differential operators called $E$-operators. By definition, an $E$-operator is the Fourier-Laplace transform of a $G$-operator. This designation is justified by the fact that the differential operator of minimal degree in $x$ of $K[x, d/dx]$ nullifying an $E$-function is the Fourier-Laplace transform of a $G$-operator [A2, 4.2].

Context-Adaptive Variable-Length Coding (CAVLC) is an entropy coding technique employed in H.264/MPEG-4 AVC video encoding. As a lossless compression method, it shares this characteristic with most entropy coders. CAVLC is used to encode residual, zig-zag ordered blocks of transform coefficients, particularly for 4x4 (and 2x2) blocks. It serves as an alternative to Context-Based Adaptive Binary Arithmetic Coding (CABAC), requiring less processing power for decoding, although it may not achieve the same level of compression efficiency. One of the key advantages of CAVLC is its universal support across all H.264 profiles, unlike CABAC, which is not supported in the Baseline and Extended profiles. CAVLC is particularly effective due to its design that leverages certain characteristics of quantized 4x4 blocks. After undergoing prediction, transformation, and quantization, these blocks typically become sparse, with most elements being zero. The highest non-zero coefficients following a zig-zag scan are often sequences of +1 or -1, which CAVLC encodes compactly. CAVLC also benefits from the correlation in the number of non-zero coefficients found in neighboring blocks. The encoding of the number of coefficients is facilitated through the use of a look-up table, with the selection of the table being dependent on the non-zero coefficients present in adjacent blocks. Furthermore, the magnitude of non-zero coefficients, known as the level, is typically higher near the start of the reordered array, close to the DC coefficient, and decreases as it moves towards higher frequencies. In summary, CAVLC is a valuable tool in video encoding for its efficiency and compatibility across various H.264 profiles, offering a balance between decoding complexity and compression performance.

ACS Medicinal Chemistry Letters is a scientific journal dedicated to the study of medicinal chemistry. Dr. Florence Sebti-Huryn is a notable figure in this field, serving as an editor for the journal Organic Reactions and contributing to the textbook "Medicinal Chemistry." Additionally, she co-authored the thought-provoking article "Medicinal Chemistry: Where Are All the Women?" which was published in the ACS Medicinal Chemistry Letters Journal. Dr. Huryn's research is centered on the design and synthesis of small molecules that can be used as probes and potential therapeutic agents for the treatment of various diseases, including cancer, neurodegenerative disorders, and infectious diseases. Her work is significant in advancing our understanding of medicinal chemistry and its applications in healthcare.

The paper presents an in-depth analysis of the error structure in sparse linear models, focusing on the impact of variance underestimation on sparsity enforcement. The authors show that although large coefficients are well approximated, smaller ones are more heavily attenuated, resulting in a selective variance underestimation phenomenon. This effect, however, is considered either harmless or advantageous in sparse linear models. The paper broadens its examination to group potentials, demonstrating that the algorithms can be readily extended to models featuring potentials of the form $ t_i(\|\vs{i}\|) $, where $ \vs{i} $ denotes a subvector of $ \vs{} $. The authors also introduce the publicly available 'glm-ie' toolbox, which implements the algorithms and techniques discussed in the paper. The toolbox is intended to be versatile and applicable across various problem domains, featuring numerous super-Gaussian potentials and allowing users to incorporate additional ones. The authors then contrast sparse Bayesian inference with point estimation for sparse linear models, highlighting the distinct goals and algorithmic characteristics of each. Sparse Bayesian inference aims to quantify uncertainty in decisions and dependencies between components, while sparse estimation seeks to eliminate unnecessary variables for efficient computation. The paper establishes a key difference between these settings, showing that exact sparsity in \( \vgamma{} \) does not occur for inference, while sparse estimation methods are characterized by fixing many \( \gamma_i \) to zero. The paper further explores the conditions for sparsity in maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation and automatic relevance determination (ARD), a sparse reconstruction method that inspired the algorithms presented in the paper. The authors demonstrate that local minimum points of SLM MAP estimation are substantially exactly sparse, with matching sparsity patterns of \( \vs{*} \) and \( \vgamma{*} \). The paper concludes by discussing the different roles of Gaussian functions in sparse estimation versus sparse inference. In sparse estimation, Gaussian functions are normalized, encouraging \( \gamma_i \to 0 \), while in variational inference, Gaussian functions lower bound \( t_i(s_i) \), with their mass vanishing as \( \gamma_i \to 0 \), providing no incentive to eliminate \( \gamma_i \). The authors suggest that type A bounding should be preferred for variational inference, while type B bounding is best suited for sparse estimation. The innovative aspects of the research include the detailed analysis of the error structure in sparse linear models, the extension to group potentials, and the development of the 'glm-ie' toolbox. The paper also provides a clear contrast between sparse Bayesian inference and point estimation, highlighting the importance of understanding the distinct goals and characteristics of each approach. The findings and results are presented in a concise and clear language, making it easier for reviewers to understand the paper.

We show that the satisfiability problem for symbolic automatic relations is undecidable by establishing that if a two-counter machine $ P $ halts after executing a sequence of instructions $ \mathbf{Code}(i_0), \mathbf{Code}(i_1), \ldots, \mathbf{Code}(i_n) $ with $ i_0 = 0 $ and $ \mathbf{Code}(i_n) = \mathbf{halt} $, then an accepting run can be derived from the execution trace. Let $ w_r $ and $ w'_r $ denote the values held in registers $ r_0 $ and $ r_1 $ throughout the execution, for $ r \in \{ 0, 1 \} $. We show that \( \conv(w_0, w_1, w'_0, w'_1) \) constitutes an accepting run. For each step \( 0 \le m \le l-1 \), where \( \mathbf{Code}(i_m) \) is not a halt instruction, transitions exist in the machine's state graph due to the construction of \( \Delta \). Specifically, $ q_{i_m} \trans{(j_{0m},j_{1m},j_{0(m+1)},j_{1(m+1)})}_{M_P} q_{i_{m+1}} $. When $ m = l $, corresponding to the halt instruction, a transition to the accept state is available: $ q_{i_m} \trans{(j_{0m}, j_{1m}, \pad, \pad)} q_{\mathrm{accept}} $. This construction utilizes the established undecidability of the halting problem for two-counter machines, thus demonstrating the undecidability of the satisfiability problem for symbolic automatic relations.

In this study, we conducted a systematic examination of the influence of five critical parameters on the imaging resolution of a lens-free on-chip digital holographic microscopy (LFOCDHM) system. These factors include the sample-to-sensor distance, the spatial and temporal coherence of the illumination, the finite size of the sensor pixels, and the finite extent of the image sub-field of view (sub-FOV) used for reconstruction. Our analysis and experiments revealed that the sensor pixel size is the most significant factor limiting the imaging resolution of LFOCDHM systems. The side effects from other experimental factors are relatively manageable. For instance, using a laser as an ideal temporally coherent light source and increasing the source-to-sample distance can approximate an ideal spatially coherent source. Employing pixel super-resolution (SR) algorithms can reduce the effective size of the imaging sensor. However, even with these measures, using an imaging sensor with smaller pixel size can still enhance the quality of the SR reconstructions. Specifically, if the desired resolution is around $1 \mu m$, the up-sampling factor $w$ will vary for different pixel sizes. When the pixel size approaches the desired resolution, the up-sampling factor $w$ will decrease, necessitating less data for reconstruction. Conversely, a greater up-sampling factor $w$ (associated with larger pixel sizes) may result in more criss-crossed frequency gaps that remain unrecoverable, even when utilizing pixel SR reconstruction algorithms. Therefore, for LFOCDHM techniques, a smaller pixel size is crucial for achieving higher resolution and requires less information to reach the expected super-resolved resolution. Additionally, using LED as the light source can make the system more compact, portable, and cost-effective. However, the coherence length of the LED will also affect the reconstructed resolution. According to our equations, increasing ${z_1}$ and decreasing ${z_2}$ can effectively improve the coherence of light sources and enhance the imaging resolution. Furthermore, decreasing ${z_2}$ can reduce the reconstructed area when the desired resolution is determined. Our analysis of these parameters based on transfer functions has provided a quantitative resolution limit determined by the minimum first cut-off frequency of these transfer functions. This quantitative relationship allows for preliminary estimates of the ultimate resolution after employing SR methods. Thus, the derived theoretical models can offer valuable guidance in selecting appropriate system parameters to achieve higher imaging resolution. To verify the theoretical models, we employed the variable-controlling approach, altering just one or two parameters in each experiment. The imaging resolution was quantified using the resolution target, and the experimental outcomes validated the accuracy of our theoretical models. It is important to note that while this work demonstrates how our theoretical models can be utilized to improve imaging resolution by optimizing the optical design of a LFOCDHM system, it may also be possible to counteract the effects of these imperfect system parameters through computational approaches. Based on the transfer functions we have derived, we can establish the forward image formation model (from object to image) for a given LFOCDHM system. Then, certain mathematical algorithms can be adopted to recover the ideal object information from the actual measurement, i.e., to solve the corresponding inverse problem. In future work, we will focus on addressing the resolution reduction associated with these factors and compensating for their adverse impact through post-processing algorithms.
